description: Locally maintained grammar lessons. Level ranges are study guidance, not certification.

concepts.title: In, on, and at
concepts.goal: Say where something is and when it happens.
rules: Use “in” for an area or a period: “in Seoul”, “in a box”, “in July”. Use “on” for a surface or a particular day: “on the table”, “on Tuesday”. Use “at” for a point or an exact time: “at the entrance”, “at 9:30”.

These are starting patterns, not rules for every phrase. Learn common expressions as units: “at home”, “at night”, “in the morning”. “In a building” stresses being inside; “at a building” can name a meeting point.

cards.label: IN
cards.example: I live in Lima.
cards.note: Lima is an area.

cards.label: ON
cards.example: The class is on Friday.
cards.note: Friday is a particular day.

cards.label: AT
cards.example: Meet me at the entrance at six.
cards.note: Both phrases identify a point.

checks.prompt: The call starts ___ 10:15 a.m.

options.feedback: Use “at” for a clock time; “on” introduces a day or date.
Use “at” for a precise clock time; “in” is used for periods such as a month.
An exact time takes “at”.

checks.prompt: The keys are resting on the table surface, not below it or inside it. Choose: “The keys are ___ the kitchen table.”

options.feedback: “Under” would put the keys below the table. They are resting on its surface.
The keys are resting on a surface.
“In” would place the keys inside something. The sentence describes a surface.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “We met in Monday.”

options.feedback: “To” does not introduce the day when a meeting happened.
Use “on” before a day of the week.
Use “on” with a named day.

application.prompt: You want to invite a friend to the library on Saturday at eleven. Which invitation uses the correct prepositions?

options.text: Meet me in the library in Saturday on eleven.
options.feedback: Use “on Saturday” and “at eleven”. “In the library” is possible, but the time phrases here are wrong.

options.text: Meet me at the library at Saturday in eleven.
options.feedback: Use “on” for Saturday and “at” for the clock time.

options.text: Meet me at the library on Saturday at eleven.
options.feedback: “At” introduces the place and clock time; “on” introduces the day.

concepts.title: Go to work, go home
concepts.goal: Describe destinations with the right phrase.
rules: Use “go to” before many destinations: “go to the station”, “go to Osaka”. Common activity expressions such as “go to work” and “go to school” usually omit the article when you mean the usual activity.

“Home”, “here”, “there”, “upstairs”, and “abroad” can work as destination adverbs: “go home”, “go there”. Do not add “to” in these patterns. “Go to the school” can mean visiting a particular school building.

cards.label: DESTINATION
cards.example: We are going to the station.
cards.note: Use “to” with the place noun.

cards.label: HOME
cards.example: I am going home.
cards.note: “Home” needs no “to” here.

cards.label: ACTIVITY
cards.example: She goes to work by bus.
cards.note: The expression names the daily activity.

checks.prompt: I am tired. I want to go ___ .

options.feedback: “Go home” does not take “to” in this meaning.
“Home” is a destination adverb here.
“At home” describes a location; “go home” describes movement.

checks.prompt: Add the missing word: “We went ___ the museum.”

options.feedback: “Go to” names the destination; “at” describes location.
“Museum” is a noun naming a destination.
“Went of” does not name a destination. Use “went to the museum”.

checks.prompt: Does “go to the school” always mean “attend classes”?

options.text: Yes. It always means being a student there.
options.feedback: Someone can go to the school to visit its building without attending classes.

options.text: No. It can mean visit the school building.
options.feedback: The article can highlight a particular place rather than the routine activity.

options.text: No. It always means working there.
options.feedback: The phrase alone does not tell us the purpose of the visit.

application.prompt: Which pair correctly describes a daily journey to work and back home?

options.text: I go work at eight. I go to home at five.
options.feedback: Use “go to work” and “go home”.

options.text: I go to work at eight. I go home at five.
options.feedback: “Go to work” uses “to”; “go home” does not.

options.text: I go to work at eight. I go at home at five.
options.feedback: “At home” describes location; movement home uses “go home”.

concepts.title: Interested or interesting?
concepts.goal: Describe a feeling and what causes it.
rules: For many pairs, the “-ed” adjective describes a feeling: “bored”, “excited”, “interested”. The “-ing” adjective describes what causes that feeling: “boring”, “exciting”, “interesting”.

People can cause feelings too. A person can be “interesting”, and a story can be “exciting”. Choose by meaning, not by whether the noun is a person or a thing. After “interested in”, use a noun or an “-ing” verb.

cards.label: FEELING
cards.example: I am interested in photography.
cards.note: This describes my feeling.

cards.label: CAUSE
cards.example: The photographer is interesting.
cards.note: This person attracts my interest.

cards.label: ACTIVITY
cards.example: I am interested in learning more.
cards.note: Use “learning” after “in”.

checks.prompt: The long wait made me feel ___ . (“bored” / “boring”)

options.feedback: Describe the feeling of the person waiting.
“Boring” describes what causes boredom. “Bored” describes the feeling here.
After “feel”, use the adjective “bored” to describe this feeling.

checks.prompt: Can a person be “interesting”?

options.text: No. Only objects can be interesting.
options.feedback: People can cause interest too: “an interesting speaker”.

options.text: Yes. It means the person feels interested.
options.feedback: “Interesting” describes the effect on others; “interested” describes the feeling.

options.text: Yes. A person can cause interest.
options.feedback: The distinction is feeling versus cause, not person versus thing.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “I am interested in learn Spanish.”

options.text: I am interesting in learning Spanish.
options.feedback: “Interested” describes your feeling. “Interesting” describes what causes interest.

options.text: I am interested in learning Spanish.
options.feedback: A verb after this preposition uses the “-ing” form.

options.text: I am interested in to learn Spanish.
options.feedback: After “in”, use the “-ing” form: “learning”.

application.prompt: Choose the sentence that describes an activity and the learner’s feeling correctly.

options.text: The class is challenging, but I feel excited about to learn.
options.feedback: After “about”, use “learning”, not “to learn”.

options.text: The class is challenging, but I feel exciting about learning.
options.feedback: “Excited” describes the learner’s feeling here.

options.text: The class is challenging, but I feel excited about learning.
options.feedback: “Challenging” describes the class; “excited” describes the feeling.

concepts.title: While and during
concepts.goal: Connect activities that overlap in time.
rules: “While” commonly introduces a clause: “while I was cooking”. “During” is a preposition followed by a noun phrase: “during dinner”. Both can locate something within another period or event.

“While cooking” is also possible when the understood subject is clear. “While” does not require a continuous tense in every context: “while I am away” is natural. “During” does not say how long an action lasted; use “for” with a duration.

cards.label: WHILE + CLAUSE
cards.example: The phone rang while I was cooking.
cards.note: A subject and verb follow “while”.

cards.label: DURING + NOUN
cards.example: The phone rang during dinner.
cards.note: “Dinner” names the event.

cards.label: FOR + DURATION
cards.example: We talked for an hour.
cards.note: “An hour” measures the duration.

checks.prompt: Choose the word meaning “at some point in the meeting”: “I took notes ___ the meeting.”

options.feedback: “The meeting” is a noun phrase.
“For the meeting” can mean intended for it; “during” identifies when the note-taking happened.
“While” normally introduces a clause here. “The meeting” is a noun phrase.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “During I was reading, it began to rain.”

options.text: While during I was reading, it began to rain.
options.feedback: Use “while” before the clause; do not add “during”.

options.text: While I was reading, it began to rain.
options.feedback: “I was reading” is a clause.

options.text: During reading I was, it began to rain.
options.feedback: The clause needs its usual order: “I was reading”, introduced by “while”.

checks.prompt: Which phrase states a measured duration: “during the lesson” or “for an hour”?

options.feedback: “During” identifies the surrounding event; “for” gives the length.

options.text: Both phrases give a measured length of time.
options.feedback: Only “for an hour” gives a measured duration.
This identifies the period when something happened, not its measured length.

application.prompt: A call interrupted your lunch preparation. Which sentence connects the two events correctly?

options.text: A friend called while I was making lunch.
options.feedback: “While” introduces the background clause “I was making lunch”.

options.text: A friend called during I was making lunch.
options.feedback: “During” takes a noun phrase; “while” introduces this clause.

options.text: A friend called while was I making lunch.
options.feedback: Use normal statement order after “while”: “I was making lunch”.

concepts.title: By and through
concepts.goal: Explain a method or a process without changing the meaning.
rules: “By” often introduces how something is done: “by checking the map”, “by train”, “by email”. “Through” can present a route, a channel, or a process: “through the park”, “through an agency”, “through regular practice”.

“By” + “-ing” and “through” + noun are useful starting patterns, not a complete rule. Both words have other uses. Both can introduce a method in some contexts: “by working together” / “through working together”. “By” highlights how; “through” can highlight the process.

cards.label: METHOD
cards.example: I saved time by booking online.
cards.note: “Booking” is the action that helped.

cards.label: PROCESS
cards.example: She gained confidence through practice.
cards.note: Practice is the process behind the change.

cards.label: ROUTE
cards.example: We walked through the station.
cards.note: “Through” describes movement from one part to another.

checks.prompt: Complete with an “-ing” form: “I checked the time by ___ at my phone.”

options.feedback: “By” takes the “-ing” form when followed by this action: “by looking”.
“Looked” is not the “-ing” form required after “by” in this pattern.
“By looking” explains the method.

checks.prompt: “We found our apartment through an agency.” How did the agency help?

options.text: The agency connected us with the apartment or its owner.
options.feedback: “Through” identifies the intermediary: someone or an organization that helps connect two sides.

options.text: The agency tells us how long the search lasted.
options.feedback: “Through an agency” identifies who helped connect the two sides, not a duration.

options.text: The agency was the route we physically walked through.
options.feedback: Here “through” identifies an intermediary, not a physical passage.

checks.prompt: Is “by” always followed by an “-ing” verb? Choose the statement with a valid example.

options.text: No. By can only be followed by a person.
options.feedback: “By email”, “by train”, and “by Friday” do not name people.

options.text: Yes. Every use of by must have an -ing verb.
options.feedback: Phrases such as “by train” and “by Friday” show that other patterns are possible.

options.text: No: by train, by email, or by Friday.
options.feedback: The form depends on the meaning and phrase.

application.prompt: Which pair correctly describes a learning method and a process that builds confidence?

options.text: I learn phrases by writing examples. I gain confidence through regular conversations.
options.feedback: “By writing” describes the method; “through conversations” identifies a helpful process.

options.text: I learn phrases by writing examples. I gain confidence through to converse.
options.feedback: “Through to converse” is not this pattern. Use “through conversations” or “through conversing”.

options.text: I learn phrases by write examples. I gain confidence through regular conversations.
options.feedback: Use the “-ing” form after “by” in this method phrase: “by writing”.

concepts.title: Nouns and verbs
concepts.goal: Choose the form that fits a sentence.
rules: A noun can name a thing, action, or idea; a verb tells what happens or describes a state. Some words have the same spelling in both roles: “a plan” / “we plan”. Other families change form: “a decision” / “decide”.

Look at the sentence pattern. An article such as “a” often comes before a noun phrase. A subject often needs a verb. Endings can help, but they are not reliable rules for every word. Check an unfamiliar word in a dictionary.

cards.label: NOUN
cards.example: We made a decision.
cards.note: “Decision” names the result.

cards.label: VERB
cards.example: We decided to wait.
cards.note: “Decided” is the past-tense verb.

cards.label: BOTH
cards.example: We plan to discuss the plan.
cards.note: The first “plan” is a verb; the second is a noun.

checks.prompt: We need to ___ today. (“decision” / “decide”)

options.feedback: After “need to”, use the verb “decide”. “Decision” is a noun.
“Decisive” is an adjective. This position needs a verb.
“To” is followed by the base verb in this pattern.

checks.prompt: Please make a ___ . (“choice” / “choose”)

options.feedback: “A” introduces a noun phrase.
The usual expression for this meaning is “make a choice”.
“Make a” takes a noun here: “choice”. “Choose” is a verb.

checks.prompt: Identify the verb: “They work at a school.”

options.feedback: “They” is the subject pronoun; “work” is the verb.
“School” is a noun in the phrase “at a school”.
“Work” tells what they do.

application.prompt: Which pair uses a verb and its related noun correctly?

options.text: We discussion the problem. The discussion was useful.
options.feedback: The first sentence needs a verb, such as “discuss” or “discussed”, rather than the noun “discussion”.

options.text: We discussed the problem. The discuss was useful.
options.feedback: After “the”, this sentence needs the noun “discussion”.

options.text: We discussed the problem. The discussion was useful.
options.feedback: “Discussed” is the past-tense verb; “discussion” is the noun.

concepts.title: About: topics and movement
concepts.goal: Use “about” for a topic and recognize its other meanings.
rules: “About” often means on the subject of: “talk about a film”, “think about a question”, “read about a place”. It does not automatically make an action longer or more detailed.

Verb patterns differ. “Discuss” normally takes its topic directly: “discuss the plan”. “Talk” usually needs “about” before a topic. “About” can also mean approximately or around a place: “about ten minutes”; “walk about the room”.

cards.label: TOPIC
cards.example: We talked about the trip.
cards.note: The trip is the subject of the conversation.

cards.label: DIRECT OBJECT
cards.example: We discussed the trip.
cards.note: No “about” is needed in this pattern.

cards.label: AROUND
cards.example: She walked about the room.
cards.note: “About” describes movement around a place.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “We discussed about the price.”

options.feedback: “Discuss” takes a direct object for its topic.
“Discuss” takes its topic directly: “discussed the price”.
Do not insert “to” between “discuss” and its topic.

checks.prompt: Does “think about” tell us how long someone thinks?

options.text: Yes. It means thinking for a long time.
options.feedback: “About” identifies the topic, not the amount of time spent thinking.
The phrase does not specify how long the thinking lasts.
Duration needs additional context, such as “for ten minutes”.

checks.prompt: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”?

options.feedback: “About” means approximately; the number could be a little higher or lower.
This is a quantity meaning, not a topic.
“About” makes the number approximate, rather than exact.

application.prompt: Which pair correctly introduces the topic after “talk” and after “discuss”?

options.text: We talked about the schedule. We discussed a possible change.
options.feedback: “Talked about” uses “about”; “discussed” takes its topic directly.

options.text: We talked about the schedule. We discussed about a possible change.
options.feedback: “Discuss” normally takes its topic directly, without “about”.

options.text: We talked about the schedule. We discussed to a possible change.
options.feedback: Do not add “to” between “discussed” and the topic.

concepts.title: Hope, expect, and possibility
concepts.goal: Separate what you want from what you think is likely.
rules: “Hope” expresses a desired outcome. “Expect” expresses a belief about what is likely. “May”, “might”, and “could” express possibility. “Will” can express a prediction, a decision, or willingness; context matters.

These words are not a fixed percentage scale. “I hope it rains” does not tell us how likely rain is. “I expect a delay” can express an unwelcome prediction. Keep facts, wishes, and uncertainty distinct.

cards.label: WISH
cards.example: I hope the train is on time.
cards.note: This is the outcome I want.

cards.label: EXPECTATION
cards.example: I expect the train to be late.
cards.note: This is what I think is likely.

cards.label: POSSIBILITY
cards.example: The train might be late.
cards.note: A delay is possible, not certain.

checks.prompt: Which expresses a wish: “I hope we win” / “I expect we will win”?

options.feedback: “Hope” identifies a desired outcome.

options.text: Both sentences say only what I wish for.
options.feedback: “Expect” adds a prediction or belief, rather than only a wish.
“Expect” reports a belief about what will happen; “hope” expresses the wish.

checks.prompt: Change this prediction to express an uncertain possibility: “The office will close early.”

options.feedback: “Must” can express necessity or a strong deduction, not a cautious possibility.
“Might” reduces the certainty. “May” or “could” also works.

options.text: The office definitely will close early.
options.feedback: “Definitely” increases certainty. The task asks for possibility.

checks.prompt: Does “I expect a problem” mean “I want one”?

options.feedback: You can expect something you do not want.

options.text: No. It expresses a belief, not a wish.
options.feedback: An expectation can be unwelcome.

options.text: No. It guarantees a problem will occur.
options.feedback: “Expect” reports a belief, not a guarantee.

application.prompt: The forecast is uncertain. Which pair separates a wish from a cautious prediction?

options.text: I expect the weather is good. It will definitely rain in the afternoon.
options.feedback: “Expect” is a belief, and “definitely rain” is not a cautious prediction.

options.text: I hope the weather is good. Rain is guaranteed in the afternoon.
options.feedback: “Guaranteed” makes the uncertain forecast sound certain.

options.text: I hope the weather is good. It might rain in the afternoon.
options.feedback: “Hope” states a wish; “might” states a possibility.

concepts.title: Because, because of, and so
concepts.goal: Give a reason and describe its result.
rules: “Because” introduces a reason with a clause: “because the bus was late”. “Because of” introduces a noun phrase: “because of the delay”. “So” can introduce the result: “The bus was late, so I walked”.
In a simple standard-English sentence, choose one clear connection rather than “because ... so ...”. A cause claim needs evidence; events happening together does not prove that one caused the other.

cards.label: BECAUSE
cards.example: I stayed home because I felt ill.
cards.note: The reason is a clause.

cards.label: BECAUSE OF
cards.example: I stayed home because of a cold.
cards.note: The reason is a noun phrase.

cards.label: RESULT
cards.example: I felt ill, so I stayed home.
cards.note: “So” introduces what happened as a result.

checks.prompt: We stopped ___ the heavy rain.

options.feedback: “So” introduces a result, whereas the rain is the reason here.
“Because” normally takes a clause; “the heavy rain” is a noun phrase.
“The heavy rain” is a noun phrase.

checks.prompt: Join with “so”: “The shop was closed. We came back later.”

options.text: The shop was closed so of we came back later.
options.feedback: “So” connects the two clauses directly; do not add “of”.

options.text: We came back later, so the shop was closed.
options.feedback: This reverses the stated reason and result.

options.text: The shop was closed, so we came back later.
options.feedback: Put the result after “so”.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “Because I was tired, so I went home.”

options.text: Because of I was tired, I went home.
options.feedback: “Because of” takes a noun phrase; “I was tired” is a clause.

options.text: Because I was tired, so of I went home.
options.feedback: Use “because” for the reason without “so of”.

options.text: Because I was tired, I went home.
options.feedback: Alternatively: “I was tired, so I went home”.

application.prompt: Your bicycle needed repair, so you took the bus. Which sentence gives that reason correctly?

options.text: My bicycle needed a repair because I took the bus.
options.feedback: This reverses the stated cause and decision.

options.text: I took the bus because my bicycle needed a repair.
options.feedback: “Because” introduces the clause giving the reason.

options.text: I took the bus because of my bicycle needed a repair.
options.feedback: “Because of” takes a noun phrase, not this full clause.

concepts.title: Adjective order
concepts.goal: Describe an object naturally without overloading the sentence.
rules: When several adjectives come before a noun, English tends to put opinion before more factual descriptions. A useful common order is opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material, purpose, then noun.

This is a tendency, not a requirement to use every category. Meaning, emphasis, and established phrases can affect order. Two or three well-chosen adjectives are usually clearer than a long stack. Use a dictionary or a natural example if an order feels uncertain.

cards.label: OPINION + SIZE
cards.example: a lovely small cafe
cards.note: An opinion comes before size.

cards.label: AGE + MATERIAL
cards.example: an old wooden chair
cards.note: Age comes before material.

cards.label: COLOR + ORIGIN
cards.example: a blue Italian jacket
cards.note: Color normally comes before origin.

checks.prompt: Choose the natural order: “bag” / “leather” / “small” / “a”

options.feedback: The article “a” normally comes before these adjectives.
Size normally comes before material.
Size normally comes before material in this neutral description.

checks.prompt: Choose the natural order: “wooden” / “old” / “an” / “table”

options.feedback: Age normally comes before material.
Age normally comes before material, and “an” does not fit before “wooden”.
The article comes first: “an old wooden table”.

checks.prompt: Must every description include all adjective categories?

options.feedback: The order is guidance for the adjectives you need.

options.text: No. You can only use one adjective for an object.
options.feedback: Two or more useful adjectives can be natural.

options.text: Yes. Each object needs every adjective category.
options.feedback: Descriptions need useful information, not every possible category.

application.prompt: The notebook is small and blue. Which description has the natural neutral order?

options.text: I keep my notes in small a blue notebook.
options.feedback: The article “a” comes before the adjectives.

options.text: I keep my notes in a large red notebook.
options.feedback: This changes the stated size and color.

options.text: I keep my notes in a small blue notebook.
options.feedback: Size normally comes before color in this description.

concepts.title: Come, go, bring, and take
concepts.goal: Describe movement from a clear point of view.
rules: “Come” often describes movement toward the speaker, listener, or an agreed meeting place. “Go” commonly describes movement away or toward another place. “Bring” and “take” describe similar movement with a person or thing.

The viewpoint can be a future location. On the phone, “I am coming to your office” treats the listener as the destination. “Bring your notes to our meeting” uses the shared meeting as the reference point. Context can make more than one choice natural.

cards.label: TOWARD US
cards.example: Can you come to my desk?
cards.note: The speaker is the destination.

cards.label: ANOTHER PLACE
cards.example: I need to go to the bank.
cards.note: The bank is another destination.

cards.label: WITH SOMETHING
cards.example: Please bring your notes to our meeting.
cards.note: The notes move toward the shared meeting.

checks.prompt: You are at home inviting a friend. Complete: “Please ___ over.”

options.feedback: “Take” normally needs something or someone being moved; it does not fit “come over”.
The speaker is inviting the friend toward the speaker’s home, so “come” fits.
The friend moves toward you.

checks.prompt: You are leaving home for class. Complete: “I must ___ my book with me.”

options.feedback: You carry the book away from your current location.
“Must” takes the base verb “take”, not the past participle “taken”.
“Must” takes a base verb, so use “take” rather than “taking”.

checks.prompt: Can “come” refer to the listener’s location?

options.text: Yes: I am coming to your office.
options.feedback: The viewpoint can be the listener or a shared destination.

options.text: Yes. Come always means movement away from both people.
options.feedback: “Come” normally uses the speaker’s, listener’s, or an agreed destination as its viewpoint.

options.text: No. Come can only mean movement to the speaker.
options.feedback: “Come” can also refer to movement toward the listener.

application.prompt: You are inviting someone to your house and asking them to carry a drink there. Which wording fits?

options.text: Come to my house for lunch. Please bringing a drink.
options.feedback: After “please”, use the base verb “bring”.

options.text: Come to my house for lunch. Please bring a drink.
options.feedback: “Come” and “bring” use the host’s destination as the viewpoint.

options.text: Come my house for lunch. Please bring a drink.
options.feedback: “Come” needs “to” before “my house”.

concepts.title: That, which, and extra information
concepts.goal: Show whether a relative clause identifies something or adds a detail.
rules: A defining relative clause identifies the noun: “The bike that has a red seat is mine”. For things, “that” and “which” can both introduce defining clauses, though some style guides prefer “that”.

A non-defining clause adds extra information and uses commas: “My bike, which has a red seat, is outside”. Use “which”, not “that”, for this extra-information pattern. For people, “who” is often appropriate. Meaning decides whether the information is defining.

cards.label: IDENTIFY
cards.example: The report that arrived today is final.
cards.note: This identifies which report.

cards.label: ADD A DETAIL
cards.example: The report, which arrived today, is final.
cards.note: The report is already identified.

cards.label: PEOPLE
cards.example: The colleague who helped me is here.
cards.note: “Who” refers to a person.

checks.prompt: Choose for extra information: “My laptop, ___ is new, works well.”

options.feedback: Use “which” for this extra-information clause set off by commas.
“What” does not replace “which” after the noun “my laptop” here.
A non-defining clause uses “which” for things.

checks.prompt: Can “which” introduce a defining clause about a thing?

options.text: Yes, although some style guides prefer that.
options.feedback: Do not mark all defining uses of “which” as ungrammatical.

options.text: Yes, but every defining which clause needs commas.
options.feedback: Commas mark extra information; a defining clause normally has no commas.

options.text: No. Which is restricted to extra information in every variety of English.
options.feedback: “Which” can also introduce a defining clause, especially in British English.

checks.prompt: Choose the punctuation for extra information: “Our office which opened in May is nearby.”

options.text: Our office, which opened in May is nearby.
options.feedback: Close the extra-information clause with a comma after “May”.

options.text: Our office, which opened in May, is nearby.
options.feedback: The commas mark the additional detail.

options.text: Our office which opened in May, is nearby.
options.feedback: Use a comma on both sides of the extra-information clause.

application.prompt: The green label is extra information about your bag. Which version shows this correctly?

options.text: My bag, which has a green label is under the chair.
options.feedback: Add a closing comma after “label”.

options.text: My bag, what has a green label, is under the chair.
options.feedback: Use “which”, not “what”, after the noun “my bag”.

options.text: My bag, which has a green label, is under the chair.
options.feedback: “Which” introduces the extra information, enclosed by two commas.

concepts.title: Allow and prohibit
concepts.goal: Explain permission and restrictions clearly.
rules: “Allow” commonly takes a person plus “to” + verb: “They allow visitors to take photos”. Without a named person, use an “-ing” form: “They allow photography / taking photos”. The passive is “be allowed to”.

“Prohibit” commonly takes an activity or person + “from” + “-ing”: “The rules prohibit parking here”; “they prohibit visitors from entering”. “Must not” expresses a prohibition. “Do not have to” expresses lack of obligation, which is different.

cards.label: PERMISSION
cards.example: Visitors are allowed to take photos.
cards.note: Taking photos is permitted.

cards.label: PROHIBITION
cards.example: Parking here is prohibited.
cards.note: Parking here is not permitted.

cards.label: NO OBLIGATION
cards.example: You do not have to print the ticket.
cards.note: Printing is optional, not forbidden.

checks.prompt: Complete: “They allow us ___ leave early.”

options.feedback: “From” would require a different pattern, such as “prevent someone from doing something”.
“Allow someone to do something” is the pattern here.
Use “allow someone to do something”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “The rule prohibits staff from ___ here.” (“smoke”)

options.feedback: Use “from smoking”, not “from to smoke”.
“From” is followed by the “-ing” form in this pattern.
Use “from” + “-ing”.

checks.prompt: Does “You do not have to wait” mean waiting is forbidden?

options.text: No. It means you are required to wait.
options.feedback: The negative “do not have to” means waiting is optional.
Use “must not wait” if it is prohibited.

options.text: Yes. It means you must not wait.
options.feedback: “Do not have to” removes necessity; “must not” expresses prohibition.

application.prompt: The kitchen is available, but leaving the door unlocked is forbidden. Which notice gives both rules?

options.text: You may use the kitchen. You do not have to leave the door unlocked.
options.feedback: “Do not have to” means not required; it does not forbid leaving the door unlocked.

options.text: You may use the kitchen. You must not leave the door unlocked.
options.feedback: “May” gives permission; “must not” gives the restriction.

options.text: You must not use the kitchen. You may leave the door unlocked.
options.feedback: This reverses both rules.

concepts.title: Past events and background actions
concepts.goal: Put a finished event in its time context.
rules: The past simple presents a finished event or a past state: “I arrived at six”; “the room was quiet”. The past continuous presents an activity in progress around a past time: “I was waiting at six”.

Combine them to show background and an event: “I was cooking when the phone rang”. This does not always mean the first activity stopped. Add “then”, “before”, or “after” when the order needs to be explicit.

cards.label: EVENT
cards.example: The bus arrived at six.
cards.note: A completed event.

cards.label: BACKGROUND
cards.example: I was waiting at the stop.
cards.note: An activity in progress.

cards.label: TOGETHER
cards.example: I was waiting when the bus arrived.
cards.note: The arrival happened during the wait.

checks.prompt: Choose: “At eight yesterday, I ___ dinner.” (“was cooking” / “cook”)

options.feedback: The time is in the past. “Was cooking” presents an activity in progress then.
“Am cooking” refers to the present, not eight yesterday.
An activity was in progress at a past time.

checks.prompt: Which happened during the walk: “I was walking when it began to rain”?

options.feedback: The walk is the background activity.

options.text: The walking began after the rain stopped.
options.feedback: The sentence says the rain began during the walk.
“Was walking” presents the walk as ongoing when the rain began.

checks.prompt: Does “was reading when the phone rang” prove the reading stopped?

options.text: Yes. Every past continuous action stops at the next event.
options.feedback: The grammatical form alone does not establish that outcome.

options.text: No. The sentence does not state that.
options.feedback: The reader may have continued.

options.text: Yes. The phone call necessarily ended the reading.
options.feedback: “When” links the events but does not state whether the person stopped reading.

application.prompt: A neighbor knocked while you were working at home yesterday. Which pair reports that background and event?

options.text: I was working at home yesterday. A neighbor knocked on the door.
options.feedback: “Was working” gives the ongoing background; “knocked” gives the event.

options.text: I am working at home yesterday. A neighbor knocks on the door.
options.feedback: “Yesterday” needs past-time forms for these reported events.

options.text: I will work at home tomorrow. A neighbor may knock on the door.
options.feedback: This changes the account into a future possibility.

concepts.title: Dates, deadlines, and durations
concepts.goal: Distinguish a deadline from a continuing period.
rules: Use “on” with a date, “in” with a month or year, and “at” with an exact time. Write the month name when a numeric date might be ambiguous across countries: “6 September 2026”.

“By Friday” means no later than Friday. “Until Friday” means continuing up to Friday. “Since” identifies a starting point; “for” gives a duration. A deadline may need a time and time zone to be clear.

cards.label: DEADLINE
cards.example: Send the form by Friday at noon.
cards.note: Friday at noon is the latest time.

cards.label: CONTINUATION
cards.example: The office is closed until Friday.
cards.note: The closed state continues up to Friday.

cards.label: DURATION
cards.example: I have lived here for two years.
cards.note: “Two years” measures the period.

checks.prompt: The appointment is ___ 6 September.

options.feedback: Use “on” for a specific date; “in” fits a month or year.
Use “on” with a particular date.
“At” fits a clock time, not the date “6 September”.

checks.prompt: Which means “no later than”: “by Friday” / “until Friday”?

options.feedback: “Until” gives the end of a continuing period. “By” gives a deadline.
“Until” describes a continuing action or state.

options.text: Both phrases always set the same deadline.
options.feedback: “By” and “until” differ: a deadline versus the end of a continuing period.

checks.prompt: Complete: “I have worked here ___ 2024.”

options.feedback: “During” identifies a period, whereas “since” identifies the starting point here.
“For” gives a duration such as “two years”; “2024” is a starting point.
The year is a starting point.

application.prompt: You need one reply no later than 3 p.m. New York time on 10 September. Which deadline is clear?

options.text: Please reply by 10 September at 3 p.m. New York time.
options.feedback: “By” gives the latest allowed time, including date and time zone.

options.text: Please reply on 10 September at three.
options.feedback: This leaves a.m./p.m. and the time zone unspecified.

options.text: Please reply until 10 September at 3 p.m. New York time.
options.feedback: “Until” suggests continuing over a period rather than the deadline for one reply.

concepts.title: Recently and lately
concepts.goal: Choose a tense that fits the event, not just the adverb.
rules: “Recently” means a short time ago or during the recent past. It can describe one finished event with the past simple: “I recently bought a bike”. It also occurs with the present perfect: “I have recently changed jobs”.

“Lately” usually describes recent states or repeated activity, often with the present perfect: “I have been busy lately”; “I have been cycling lately”. It is less usual for a single finished event. Neither word requires the present perfect continuous, and neither guarantees that an activity will continue.

cards.label: ONE EVENT
cards.example: I recently visited a friend.
cards.note: Past simple fits a finished visit.

cards.label: RECENT STATE
cards.example: I have been tired lately.
cards.note: “Been” + adjective describes a state.

cards.label: REPEATED ACTIVITY
cards.example: I have been walking more lately.
cards.note: The continuous form highlights activity.

checks.prompt: Choose for a single visit: “I visited Rome ___ .” (“recently” / “lately”)

options.feedback: “Recent” is an adjective; this sentence needs an adverb.
“Recently” is the usual choice with this single past-simple visit.
“Recently” readily refers to a single past event.

checks.prompt: Is “I have been busy lately” a present perfect continuous verb?

options.text: No. It is present perfect be followed by an adjective.
options.feedback: The continuous form needs an “-ing” main verb.

options.text: Yes. Every phrase with have been is continuous.
options.feedback: Continuous forms need an “-ing” main verb. “Busy” is an adjective.

options.text: No. It is the past perfect.
options.feedback: Past perfect would use “had”; “have been” is present perfect here.

checks.prompt: Does “I have been running lately” guarantee future running?

options.feedback: Future continuation needs more context.
“Lately” refers to the recent past, not a guaranteed future.

options.text: Yes. It promises the person will keep running.
options.feedback: A report of recent activity does not promise future activity.

application.prompt: Which pair naturally describes one recent event and a recent repeated activity?

options.text: I recently joined a class. I have studying more lately.
options.feedback: The continuous form needs “been”: “have been studying”.

options.text: I lately joined a class. I have been studying more lately.
options.feedback: “Recently” is the usual choice for this single past-simple event.

options.text: I recently joined a class. I have been studying more lately.
options.feedback: “Recently” fits the single event; “lately” fits the recent pattern of studying.

concepts.title: Suggest and recommend
concepts.goal: Offer an idea using a natural verb pattern.
rules: Use “suggest” or “recommend” with a noun or an “-ing” activity: “suggest a cafe”; “recommend booking early”. With a named person doing the action, a “that” clause is useful: “I suggest that she book early”. “She should book” is also possible after “that”, especially in British English.

Do not use “suggest someone to do” for advice. Say “suggest that someone do”, or “suggest doing”. “Recommend” has additional patterns and meanings, such as “recommend someone for a job”. Learn the meaning and pattern together instead of treating both verbs as identical in every use.

cards.label: ACTIVITY
cards.example: I recommend booking ahead.
cards.note: “Booking” is the suggested activity.

cards.label: PERSON + ACTION
cards.example: I suggest that Mina call first.
cards.note: Use the base verb “call” in this advice pattern.

cards.label: RECIPIENT
cards.example: She suggested a cafe to me.
cards.note: “To me” identifies the recipient of the suggestion.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “She suggested me to apply.”

options.feedback: “Suggest” does not use the person + to-infinitive advice pattern.

options.text: She suggested that I to apply.
options.feedback: After “suggested that I”, use the base verb “apply” without “to”.

options.text: She suggested to me to apply.
options.feedback: Use “suggested to me that I apply”, or “suggested that I apply”, for this meaning.

checks.prompt: Complete: “I recommend ___ early.” (“arrive”)

options.feedback: Use an “-ing” form for the activity.
“Recommend” takes the “-ing” form in this pattern: “recommend arriving”.
Do not combine “to” with “arriving” in this pattern.

checks.prompt: Is “I suggest that she should call” possible?

options.feedback: “Should” + base verb is an accepted alternative.

options.text: Yes, but only when giving advice about the past.
options.feedback: The pattern can give advice about a present or future action.

options.text: No. Should is forbidden after suggest.
options.feedback: “Suggest that someone should do something” is an established pattern.

application.prompt: Which recommendation uses a standard “suggest” pattern?

options.text: I suggest taking an earlier train so you have time to find the office.
options.feedback: “Suggest” can take an “-ing” form: “taking”.

options.text: I suggest that you to take an earlier train.
options.feedback: Use “suggest that you take”, without “to”.

options.text: I suggest you should taking an earlier train.
options.feedback: “Should” takes the base verb “take”, not “taking”.

concepts.title: Where to put only
concepts.goal: Make clear what you are limiting.
rules: “Only” limits a person, thing, action, amount, or time. Put it close to the element you want to limit when clarity matters: “Only Jo called” means nobody else called; “Jo called only Sam” means Sam was the only recipient.

In speech, stress and context also shape the meaning. “I only bought two” can be understood naturally even if “only” is not immediately before “two”. Do not assume every everyday placement is wrong; revise when a reader could misunderstand.

cards.label: PERSON
cards.example: Only Jo called Sam.
cards.note: Nobody other than Jo called Sam.

cards.label: RECIPIENT
cards.example: Jo called only Sam.
cards.note: Jo called no one except Sam.

cards.label: ACTION
cards.example: Jo only called; she did not visit.
cards.note: The action was limited to a call.

checks.prompt: Which says Sam was the sole recipient: “Only Jo called Sam” / “Jo called only Sam”?

options.feedback: This makes Jo the only caller, not Sam the only recipient.

options.text: Both sentences make Sam the only recipient.
options.feedback: The position of “only” changes which person is singled out.
“Only” limits Sam.

checks.prompt: Choose the sentence with the same meaning: “No one except Leo replied.”

options.feedback: This introduces Ana and does not say that no one else replied.
“Only” is next to the person being limited.
This can restrict what Leo did, not identify Leo as the sole person replying.

checks.prompt: Can spoken stress help clarify “only”?

options.text: Yes. Stress makes written word order irrelevant.
options.feedback: Speech can clarify focus, but careful word order still helps written readers.

options.text: No. Spoken stress never affects meaning.
options.feedback: Stress can show which part of the sentence “only” limits.

options.text: Yes. Stress and context can identify the focus.
options.feedback: In writing, a clearer position may help.

application.prompt: Which pair moves “only” so the first sentence limits the person and the second limits the drink?

options.text: Ana ordered only tea. Only Ana ordered tea.
options.feedback: These meanings occur in the opposite order.

options.text: Only Ana ordered tea. Only Ana ordered coffee.
options.feedback: “Only” limits Ana in both sentences; it does not switch to limiting the drink.

options.text: Only Ana ordered tea. Ana ordered only tea.
options.feedback: The first singles out Ana; the second singles out tea.

concepts.title: Directions and locations
concepts.goal: Help someone locate a place or an item.
rules: Use “north”, “south”, “east”, and “west” for compass directions. “Northeast” combines “north” and “east”. On a map, check the orientation rather than assuming the top is always north.

Use “top”, “bottom”, “left”, and “right” to describe positions on a page or object: “in the top-left corner”; “at the bottom of the page”. A place can be “in the north of a country” or “north of another place”; these describe different relationships.

cards.label: WITHIN AN AREA
cards.example: The town is in the north of the country.
cards.note: It lies inside the northern part.

cards.label: RELATIVE POSITION
cards.example: The station is north of the park.
cards.note: Compare the station with the park.

cards.label: ON A PAGE
cards.example: The address is in the top-right corner.
cards.note: This describes a page position.

checks.prompt: Which direction combines north and east?

options.feedback: “Southeast” combines “south” and “east”.
The two compass directions combine into one word.
“Northwest” combines “north” and “west”, not “north” and “east”.

checks.prompt: Where is something described as “at the bottom of the page”?

options.text: Near the lower edge of the page.
options.feedback: “Bottom” describes a position on the page.

options.text: Near the upper edge of the page.
options.feedback: The bottom is the lower edge; the top is the upper edge.

options.text: Outside the page on its right side.
options.feedback: “At the bottom” identifies a lower position on the page.

checks.prompt: Does “north of the city” mean inside the city?

options.text: No. It tells us the exact distance from the city.
options.feedback: “North of” gives direction, not a measured distance.

options.text: Yes. It must be inside the northern part of the city.
options.feedback: “North of” gives a position relative to the city; inside it is not guaranteed.

options.text: Not necessarily. It gives a position relative to the city.
options.feedback: “In the north of the city” explicitly places it inside the city.

application.prompt: The station is east of the park and its label is in the map’s top-right corner. Which description preserves both details?

options.text: The station is west of the park. Its label is in the top-right corner of the map.
options.feedback: “West” reverses the stated direction.

options.text: The station is east of the park. Its label is in the top-right corner of the map.
options.feedback: The first phrase locates the station; the second locates its label on the map.

options.text: The station is east of the park. Its label is in the bottom-left corner of the map.
options.feedback: This changes the label’s position.

concepts.title: Asking about prices
concepts.goal: Ask what something costs and clarify the total.
rules: Use “How much is it?” for one item and “How much are they?” for plural items. With “cost” as a verb, use “does” for one item: “How much does it cost?” The main verb stays in its base form after “does”.

Ask what the price includes when you need the total. “Price”, “cost”, “fee”, and “fare” fit different contexts: “a course fee”, “a bus fare”. Do not assume that a displayed amount includes every charge.

cards.label: BE
cards.example: How much is this notebook?
cards.note: One item takes “is”.

cards.label: COST
cards.example: How much do these tickets cost?
cards.note: Plural tickets take “do”.

cards.label: CLARIFY
cards.example: Does that include delivery?
cards.note: Ask what is included in the stated amount.

checks.prompt: Complete: “How much ___ these shoes?”

options.feedback: “Shoes” is plural.
“These shoes” is plural, so use “are”.
With “these shoes”, use “are”, or ask “How much do these shoes cost?”

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “How much does it costs?”

options.feedback: “Does” carries the third-person ending; “cost” stays in the base form.
“It” takes “does”, not “do”.
After “does”, use the base verb “cost”.

checks.prompt: Which question asks whether delivery is included in the price?

options.feedback: This asks about timing, not what the price includes.
This asks the delivery price, not whether it is included.
The question makes the total clearer.

application.prompt: Which exchange asks the price and then checks whether delivery is included?

options.text: How much is the desk? It is eighty dollars. Does that include delivery?
options.feedback: “How much” asks the price; “does that include” checks what the price covers.

options.text: How much does the desk costs? It is eighty dollars. Does that include delivery?
options.feedback: After “does”, use “cost” without “-s”.

options.text: How much is the desk? It is eighty dollars. Delivery is definitely free.
options.feedback: The last sentence assumes free delivery instead of checking.

concepts.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
concepts.goal: Talk about amounts using the right noun pattern.
rules: Countable nouns can have singular and plural forms: “a chair”, “two chairs”. Uncountable uses describe a mass or general idea: “some furniture”, “some advice”. Use “a piece of advice” or “an item of furniture” to count units.

Countability belongs to a use, not always to a word forever. “Coffee” can be a drink in general or a countable serving: “two coffees”. Use a dictionary to check unfamiliar meanings. “Information”, “advice”, and “equipment” are normally uncountable in general English.

cards.label: COUNT
cards.example: We need three chairs.
cards.note: Individual chairs can be counted.

cards.label: AMOUNT
cards.example: We need some furniture.
cards.note: “Furniture” is normally uncountable.

cards.label: UNIT
cards.example: She gave me two pieces of advice.
cards.note: “Pieces” provides a countable unit.

checks.prompt: Choose: “a useful information” / “some useful information”

options.feedback: For individual units, say “two pieces of information”.
“Information” is normally uncountable.
“Information” is normally uncountable; use “some information” or “a piece of information”.

checks.prompt: Which phrase correctly counts two units of advice?

options.feedback: Use a unit expression rather than “advices”.
“Advice” is normally uncountable; count “pieces of advice”.
Use a unit phrase: “two pieces of advice”.

checks.prompt: Can “two coffees” be natural in a cafe?

options.text: No. Coffee can never be used as a countable noun.
options.feedback: In a cafe, “coffees” can mean servings.

options.text: Yes. It always means two types of coffee beans.
options.feedback: “Two coffees” can simply mean two drinks, not necessarily different types.

options.text: Yes. It can mean two servings of coffee.
options.feedback: A word can have a countable use in a particular context.

application.prompt: You need two chairs and an unspecified amount of storage furniture. Which sentence states this correctly?

options.text: I need two chair and some furniture for storage.
options.feedback: After “two”, use plural “chairs”.

options.text: I need two chairs and two furnitures for storage.
options.feedback: Use “pieces of furniture” to count units of furniture.

options.text: I need two chairs and some furniture for storage.
options.feedback: “Chairs” is countable; “furniture” is normally uncountable.

concepts.title: Measurements and shapes
concepts.goal: Describe size with an appropriate unit and pattern.
rules: Use an adjective after the measurement: “The table is two meters long”. Use a noun with “of”: “a length of two meters”. In a compound adjective before a noun, the unit is singular: “a two-meter table”.

Choose the dimension you mean: “long” for length, “wide” for width, “high” or “tall” for height, and “deep” for depth. “Tall” is common for people and upright objects. Use “square”, “round”, or “rectangular” for shape. Always include the unit when a number alone is unclear.

cards.label: AFTER THE NOUN
cards.example: The cable is three meters long.
cards.note: The measurement describes the cable.

cards.label: BEFORE THE NOUN
cards.example: It is a three-meter cable.
cards.note: The unit stays singular in this compound adjective.

cards.label: SHAPE
cards.example: The table is rectangular.
cards.note: “Rectangular” describes shape, not size.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “a five-meters cable”

options.feedback: Use the singular unit in a compound adjective.
The measurement adjective uses “meter”, not “metered”, for this meaning.
In a compound adjective before a noun, use the singular unit: “five-meter-long”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “The pool is two meters ___ .” (“depth” / “deep”)

options.feedback: “Deeply” is an adverb, not the dimension adjective needed here.
The sentence needs the adjective “deep”. “Depth” is a noun.
An adjective follows this measurement.

checks.prompt: What information is missing from “The desk is 120 wide”?

options.feedback: The number needs a unit to be useful.
The missing information is the unit used to measure the width.

options.text: An opinion about the desk’s color.
options.feedback: A numerical dimension needs its measurement unit.

application.prompt: The desk is 120 centimeters wide and has a rectangular top. Which description is complete and grammatical?

options.text: My desk is 120 centimeters width. Its top is rectangular.
options.feedback: Use “wide” as the dimension adjective; “width” is a noun.

options.text: My desk is 120 wide. Its top is rectangular.
options.feedback: The numerical width needs its unit.

options.text: My desk is 120 centimeters wide. Its top is rectangular.
options.feedback: The description includes the value, measurement unit, and shape adjective.

concepts.title: All, each, every, and none
concepts.goal: Describe a whole group or its individual members.
rules: “All” usually treats the group together: “All the students are here”. “Each” and “every” normally take a singular noun and singular verb: “Each student has a book”; “every room is ready”. “Each” highlights individuals; “every” emphasizes the whole set.

Use “each of the students”, not “every of the students”. “None of” takes a plural or uncountable noun phrase. With a plural noun, either singular or plural agreement can occur depending on meaning and style: “None of the seats is/are free”.

cards.label: GROUP
cards.example: All the rooms are ready.
cards.note: The rooms are considered together.

cards.label: INDIVIDUALS
cards.example: Each room has a key.
cards.note: Consider the rooms one by one.

cards.label: ZERO
cards.example: None of the water is clean.
cards.note: The uncountable “water” takes “is”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “Every student ___ a notebook.” (“has” / “have”)

options.feedback: “Every student” takes singular agreement: “has”.
This sentence needs a finite verb: “has”.
“Every” + singular noun normally takes a singular verb.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “Every of the rooms is ready.”

options.text: Every of the rooms are ready.
options.feedback: “Every of” is not the pattern. Use “each of” or “every room”.

options.text: Each of the rooms is ready.
options.feedback: Alternatively: “Every room is ready”.

options.text: Each of the room is ready.
options.feedback: After “each of the”, use the plural noun “rooms”.

checks.prompt: Must “None of the seats are free” always be changed to “is”?

options.text: Yes. None always requires a singular verb.
options.feedback: With a plural noun, plural agreement with “none” is accepted.

options.text: No. None of the seats means all the seats are free.
options.feedback: “None of the seats are free” means there are no free seats.

options.text: No. Plural agreement is accepted with a plural noun.
options.feedback: Meaning and style can guide the choice.

application.prompt: Every student has a pencil, and there are no calculators in the group. Which pair states this correctly?

options.text: Every student has a pencil. None of the students has a calculator.
options.feedback: “Every student” takes “has”. “None of the students has a calculator” is acceptable; “have” is also possible after “none of the students”.

options.text: Every student have a pencil. None of the students has a calculator.
options.feedback: “Every student” requires singular “has”.

options.text: Every student has a pencil. All of the students have a calculator.
options.feedback: The second sentence contradicts the stated absence of calculators.

concepts.title: Accuse and blame
concepts.goal: Distinguish an allegation from an assignment of responsibility.
rules: “Accuse someone of something” means say that the person did something wrong: “accuse someone of lying”. “Blame someone for something” assigns responsibility: “blame the supplier for a delay”. Another pattern is “blame something on someone or something”: “blame the delay on a missed delivery”.

An accusation is a claim, not proof. Use “alleged”, “said”, or “according to” when reporting an unestablished claim. In a practical discussion, describing an observed problem and asking for an explanation can be more useful than assigning blame.

cards.label: ACCUSE OF
cards.example: They accused him of sharing the file.
cards.note: They claimed he did something wrong.

cards.label: BLAME ON
cards.example: They blamed the delay on a missed delivery.
cards.note: This assigns a cause.

cards.label: OBSERVE
cards.example: The file arrived after the deadline.
cards.note: This states an observable event.

checks.prompt: Complete: “She accused him ___ copying.”

options.feedback: “Accuse someone” takes “of” before the alleged action.
The pattern is “accuse someone of something”. “Blame someone for” is a different pattern.
The pattern is “accuse someone of something”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “They blamed me ___ the mistake.”

options.feedback: Use “blame someone for something”.
The pattern is “blame someone for something”; “accuse someone of” is different.
Use “for” to introduce the matter someone is blamed for.

checks.prompt: Does “was accused of” prove that someone did it?

options.text: No. It proves the person did not do it.
options.feedback: The accusation alone proves neither guilt nor innocence.
Keep the distinction between a claim and an established fact.

options.text: Yes. An accusation proves the action happened.
options.feedback: An accusation is an allegation, not proof.

application.prompt: You only know that the report arrived late. Which response gives that observation and asks for missing information?

options.text: The report arrived after the deadline because you ignored it.
options.feedback: The stated facts do not establish that cause.

options.text: You deliberately delayed the report. Why did you do that?
options.feedback: “Deliberately” assigns an intention that the facts do not establish.

options.text: The report arrived after the deadline. What caused the delay?
options.feedback: This states the observed fact and asks about the cause without assigning blame.

concepts.title: Negatives and their scope
concepts.goal: Make clear what is not true or not required.
rules: In standard written English, combine “not” with “any” or use “no”: “I do not have any cash” / “I have no cash”. Other dialects use negative concord, such as “not ... nothing”; recognize it without treating its speakers as less capable.

Position changes scope. “Not everyone came” means some people did not come; “nobody came” means zero people came. “Must not” means prohibited, while “do not have to” means optional. Check what part of the meaning you are negating.

cards.label: PART OF A GROUP
cards.example: Not everyone agreed.
cards.note: At least one person did not agree.

cards.label: ZERO
cards.example: Nobody agreed.
cards.note: No person agreed.

cards.label: OPTIONAL
cards.example: You do not have to attend.
cards.note: Attendance is not required.

checks.prompt: Choose the standard formal-English version: “I do not have no time.”

options.text: I do not have any time.
options.feedback: Alternatively: “I have no time”.
Without the negative, this does not express the intended lack of time.

options.text: I do not have some no time.
options.feedback: For this standard negative, use “do not have any time”.

checks.prompt: Does “Not all seats are taken” mean every seat is empty?

options.text: No. It means every seat is occupied.
options.feedback: That would mean all seats are taken, the opposite of “not all”.

options.text: No. It means at least some seats are free.
options.feedback: “Not all” and “none” have different meanings.

options.text: Yes. It means no seats are occupied.
options.feedback: “Not all” denies that every seat is taken; some can still be occupied.

checks.prompt: Which means “prohibited”: “must not” / “do not have to”?

options.text: Both mean the action is forbidden.
options.feedback: “Must not” forbids; “do not have to” makes the action optional.
This means not required, not prohibited.
“Do not have to” removes an obligation.

application.prompt: Printing the form is optional; sharing a password is forbidden. Which wording matches?

options.text: You must not print the form. You do not have to share your password.
options.feedback: This forbids printing and makes sharing optional, changing both rules.

options.text: You have to print the form. You must not share your password.
options.feedback: “Have to” makes printing required, contrary to the stated rule.

options.text: You do not have to print the form. You must not share your password.
options.feedback: “Do not have to” removes necessity; “must not” prohibits an action.

concepts.title: The past perfect
concepts.goal: Show what had happened before another past point.
rules: Form the past perfect with “had” + past participle: “had left”, “had seen”, “had finished”. It looks back from a past reference point to an earlier event or state.

Use it when the order or earlier background matters. It is not required for every earlier event if “before”, “after”, or context already makes the sequence clear. The negative is “had not” + participle; a question begins with “Had” + subject.

cards.label: EARLIER EVENT
cards.example: The train had left when I arrived.
cards.note: The departure happened before the arrival.

cards.label: EARLIER STATE
cards.example: I had never visited before that trip.
cards.note: Look back from the time of the trip.

cards.label: QUESTION
cards.example: Had you booked before you called?
cards.note: “Had” comes before the subject.

checks.prompt: Complete: “She had ___ before I arrived.” (“leave”)

options.feedback: “Had leaving” is not the past perfect form of “leave”.
Use the past participle after “had”.
“Had” takes the past participle “left” in this pattern.

checks.prompt: What happened first: “I had eaten when the guests arrived”?

options.feedback: “Had eaten” places the eating before their arrival.
“Had eaten” places the meal before the arrival.

options.text: The two actions necessarily started together.
options.feedback: Past perfect places the eating earlier; it does not mean simultaneous starts.

checks.prompt: Is the past perfect always required after the conjunction “after”?

options.text: No. Past perfect can never be used with after.
options.feedback: Past perfect is possible when emphasizing an earlier completed action.

options.text: No. After can already make the order clear.
options.feedback: “After I finished, I left” is natural.
“After” can make the sequence clear even with past-simple verbs.

application.prompt: The shop closed before you arrived. Which sentence makes that order clear?

options.text: The shop closed after I reached it.
options.feedback: “After” reverses the stated order.

options.text: When I reached the shop, it had already closed.
options.feedback: “Had already closed” places the closure before the arrival.

options.text: When I reached the shop, it would close tomorrow.
options.feedback: This places the closure in the future instead.

concepts.title: Few, a few, little, and a little
concepts.goal: Express a small amount with the intended emphasis.
rules: Use “few” and “a few” for small numbers of countable plural nouns. Use “little” and “a little” for small amounts of an uncountable noun. “Few”/“little” often stress a shortage; “a few”/“a little” stress that some are available.

Context decides whether an amount is enough. “A few” does not promise a sufficient number. “Little” can also be an adjective meaning small, as in “little houses” or “little people”; that is a different use from the quantity word.

cards.label: SMALL NUMBER
cards.example: I have a few questions.
cards.note: There are some questions.

cards.label: SHORTAGE
cards.example: We have little time.
cards.note: The speaker emphasizes the small amount.

cards.label: SOME AVAILABLE
cards.example: We have a little time.
cards.note: The speaker emphasizes that some time remains.

checks.prompt: Choose for an amount: “a little advice” / “a few advice”

options.feedback: “Advice” is normally uncountable.
“Advice” is normally uncountable; use “a little advice” or “a few pieces of advice”.
Do not add a plural ending to “advice” in this use.

checks.prompt: Which usually sounds more positive: “few friends” / “a few friends”?

options.feedback: “Few” often emphasizes a shortage; “a few” emphasizes that some exist.

options.text: Both always communicate exactly the same attitude.
options.feedback: Adding “a” often changes the emphasis from a shortage to a small positive amount.
It emphasizes having some friends.

checks.prompt: Must “little houses” mean a small number of houses?

options.text: Yes. Little always counts how many houses there are.
options.feedback: “Little” before “houses” normally describes their size.

options.text: No. It normally means small houses.
options.feedback: “Little” can describe physical size.

options.text: No. It normally means expensive houses.
options.feedback: “Little” describes small size, not price.

application.prompt: Which sentence correctly expresses a small amount of time tonight and a shortage of free hours this week?

options.text: I have a little time this evening, but little free hours this week.
options.feedback: “Hours” is countable and plural, so use “few” for the shortage.

options.text: I have a little time this evening, but few free hours this week.
options.feedback: “A little” goes with uncountable “time”; “few” emphasizes a shortage of countable “hours”.

options.text: I have a few time this evening, but few free hours this week.
options.feedback: “Time” is uncountable here, so use “a little”.

concepts.title: This, that, and it
concepts.goal: Refer clearly to objects and ideas in context.
rules: “This” and “that” can point to objects or refer to ideas. “This” often presents something as near or currently in focus; “that” can refer back or suggest greater distance. The distance may be physical, conversational, or emotional.

Either speaker can use “this” or “that”. There is no rule that “this” must refer to your own idea and “that” to someone else’s. “It” often continues a reference to an identified thing or situation. Name the idea again when a pronoun would be unclear.

cards.label: IN FOCUS
cards.example: This is my main concern: the cost.
cards.note: “This” introduces the idea in focus.

cards.label: REFER BACK
cards.example: I missed the train. That made me late.
cards.note: The same speaker refers back to their own statement.

cards.label: CONTINUE
cards.example: I bought a bag. It is very light.
cards.note: “It” continues the reference to the bag.

checks.prompt: Can the same speaker say “I lost my key. That was frustrating”?

options.text: No. That can only refer to a physical object.
options.feedback: “That” can also refer to situations, statements, and events.

options.text: No. That can only refer to someone else’s event.
options.feedback: “That” can refer back to an event the same speaker just described.

options.text: Yes. That can refer back to the speaker’s own event.
options.feedback: Pronoun choice is not determined by who first mentioned the idea.

checks.prompt: What does “it” refer to in “I found a notebook. It was empty”?

options.feedback: In this sentence “it” refers back to the notebook, not the speaker.
“Empty” describes the notebook here, not the act of finding it.
“It” continues an identified reference.

checks.prompt: Improve the unclear “It was a problem” after mentioning two possible problems.

options.feedback: Changing “it” to “that” may leave the same uncertainty about which problem is meant.

options.text: Name the problem, for example: The missing address was a problem.
options.feedback: A noun phrase removes the ambiguous reference.
“Definitely” strengthens the claim without clarifying what it refers to.

application.prompt: A canceled bus made you walk home. Which pair refers clearly to that event and its consequence?

options.text: The bus was canceled. That meant I had to walk home.
options.feedback: “That” refers back to the cancellation event.

options.text: The bus was delayed. That meant I had to walk home.
options.feedback: This changes the stated cancellation into a delay. Preserve the original event.

options.text: The bus was canceled and the taxi was late. It meant I had to walk home.
options.feedback: “It” could refer to either the cancellation or the late taxi. Name the event or use a reference that clearly points to the bus cancellation.

concepts.title: To do and for doing
concepts.goal: Explain a purpose or the function of an object.
rules: Use “to” + base verb to explain an action’s purpose: “I went out to buy bread”. Use “for” + noun for a purpose or recipient: “a bag for groceries”; “a gift for Lee”.

“For” + “-ing” often describes a function: “a tool for opening bottles”. A to-infinitive can also describe a use: “something to open bottles with”. Do not use “for buying” to explain why you went out in the basic “I went out to buy” pattern.

cards.label: PURPOSE OF ACTION
cards.example: I called to ask a question.
cards.note: “To ask” gives the reason for calling.

cards.label: FUNCTION
cards.example: This brush is for cleaning shoes.
cards.note: “For cleaning” describes the use.

cards.label: RECIPIENT
cards.example: This message is for Ana.
cards.note: Ana is the intended recipient.

checks.prompt: Complete: “I am saving money ___ buy a bike.”

options.feedback: “For buy” is not the purpose pattern. Use “to buy”.
Use the infinitive to express the purpose of saving.
Use “to buy” without adding “for” in this standard pattern.

checks.prompt: Complete: “This tool is for ___ cans.” (“open”)

options.feedback: The function is expressed with “for opening”, not the past form.
“For” takes the “-ing” form here: “for opening”.
A verb after “for” takes the “-ing” form.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “I went to the shop for buy milk.”

options.text: I went to the shop to buy milk.
options.feedback: “To buy” explains the purpose of the trip.

options.text: I went to the shop to buying milk.
options.feedback: After “to” in this infinitive, use the base verb “buy”.

options.text: I went to the shop for to buy milk.
options.feedback: Use “to buy” in this standard purpose sentence.

application.prompt: Which pair correctly gives a purpose for a bottle and the function of a brush?

options.text: I bought a bottle to carry water. This small brush is for cleaning it.
options.feedback: “To carry” gives the purpose; “for cleaning” gives the brush’s function.

options.text: I bought a bottle to carry water. This small brush is for to cleaning it.
options.feedback: Use “for cleaning”, without “to”.

options.text: I bought a bottle for carry water. This small brush is for cleaning it.
options.feedback: Use “to carry” to express this purpose.

concepts.title: So and so that
concepts.goal: Distinguish a result from an intended purpose.
rules: “So” commonly introduces a result: “I was tired, so I went home”. “So that” commonly introduces a purpose, often with “can”, “could”, “will”, or “would”: “I wrote it down so that I could remember it”.

“That” is sometimes omitted in informal purpose clauses: “I wrote it down so I could remember”. Use context to decide the meaning. “In order to” takes a base verb; “in order that” takes a clause and is more formal. A purpose does not guarantee success.

cards.label: RESULT
cards.example: The train stopped, so we got off.
cards.note: Getting off followed the stop.

cards.label: PURPOSE
cards.example: I left early so that I could find a seat.
cards.note: Finding a seat was the goal.

cards.label: INFINITIVE
cards.example: I left early in order to find a seat.
cards.note: The same purpose uses “to” + verb.

checks.prompt: Result or purpose: “I spoke slowly so that everyone could follow”?

options.feedback: A purpose does not guarantee the intended result happened.
“So that everyone could follow” states the speaker’s aim.
The speaker intended to help understanding.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “I called in order to that I could ask.”

options.text: I called in order that to ask.
options.feedback: Use either “in order to ask” or “so that I could ask”.

options.text: I called so that I could ask.
options.feedback: Alternatively: “I called in order to ask”.
“So that” normally introduces a clause with a subject and verb.

checks.prompt: Does “left early so that I could get a seat” prove I got one?

options.text: Yes. A purpose clause proves success.
options.feedback: The clause states the aim; it does not establish the actual result.
The intended result may not have happened.

options.text: No. It proves there were no seats.
options.feedback: The outcome is not stated either way.

application.prompt: You left early to catch a bus, but it was full. Which pair separates your purpose from the actual outcome?

options.text: I left early so that I could catch the bus. It was full, so I waited for the next one.
options.feedback: “So that” gives the aim; “so” introduces the consequence of the bus being full.

options.text: I left early because of I could catch the bus. It was full.
options.feedback: “Because of” does not introduce a full clause.

options.text: I left early so that I could catch the bus. That proves I got on it.
options.feedback: A purpose clause does not prove success, and the stated outcome says you did not board.

concepts.title: Saying times and making appointments
concepts.goal: Agree on an unambiguous time.
rules: You can say 9:15 as “nine fifteen” or “a quarter past nine”. 9:45 can be “nine forty-five” or “a quarter to ten”. Digital forms are often easiest when confirming an appointment.

Use “a.m.” or “p.m.” when the part of the day is unclear. Noon is midday; midnight is the start of a new day in date-based schedules. Include the date and time zone for an international meeting. Confirm rather than guess.

cards.label: PAST THE HOUR
cards.example: a quarter past nine

cards.label: BEFORE THE HOUR
cards.example: a quarter to ten

cards.label: CONFIRM
cards.example: Is that 9 a.m. Tokyo time?
cards.note: Clarify the time zone and part of day.

checks.prompt: Which time is “half past two”?

options.feedback: “Half past” means thirty minutes after the hour.
“Half past” means 30 minutes after the hour, not 15.
“Half past two” is 30 minutes after two, not before it.

checks.prompt: Which time is “a quarter to six”?

options.feedback: It is fifteen minutes before six.
6:45 is “a quarter to seven”, not six.
“A quarter to six” is 15 minutes before six; 6:15 is “a quarter past”.

checks.prompt: What should you clarify in “Let’s meet at eight” if you are in different countries?

options.text: The date, a.m. or p.m., and time zone.
options.feedback: A complete appointment avoids assumptions.

options.text: Only whether eight is written as a digit or a word.
options.feedback: The possible confusion is the actual date and time zone, not the spelling.

options.text: Only the length of the meeting.
options.feedback: Duration does not clarify when the meeting starts.

application.prompt: Which message gives an exact appointment date and time and asks about the time zone?

options.text: Let’s meet soon. Is that London time?
options.feedback: “Soon” does not give the required date and clock time.

options.text: Let’s meet on 12 September at 10 a.m. Is that London time?
options.feedback: It includes the date, clock time, “a.m.”, and a time-zone check.

options.text: Let’s meet on 12 September at ten. I will see you then.
options.feedback: “Ten” leaves “a.m.”/“p.m.” unclear, and no time zone is checked.

concepts.title: Even if and even though
concepts.goal: Distinguish a condition from an accepted fact.
rules: “Even though” introduces a fact accepted in the sentence: “Even though it was raining, we walked”. “Even if” introduces a condition or possibility that does not change the result: “Even if it rains, we will walk”.

The “if” clause does not assert that the condition is true. It can refer to a possibility or something already known in context; its job is conditional. For a likely future condition, normally use present tense after “if” rather than “will”.

cards.label: ACCEPTED FACT
cards.example: Even though I was tired, I stayed.
cards.note: The speaker says they were tired.

cards.label: CONDITION
cards.example: Even if I am tired, I will stay.
cards.note: The plan holds whether or not I am tired.

cards.label: CONTRAST
cards.example: It was expensive, but I bought it.
cards.note: “But” can express a simpler contrast.

checks.prompt: Which asserts rain occurred: “Even if it rained” / “Even though it rained”?

options.text: Both phrases assert that it rained.
options.feedback: “Even if” can discuss a condition without asserting it happened.
“Even if” presents a condition; “even though” presents a conceded fact.
“Even though” presents the rain as a fact.

checks.prompt: Complete: “Even if she ___ late, we will wait.” (“arrive”)

options.feedback: The clause needs a finite verb: “she arrives”.
Use present simple for this future condition.
“She” takes “arrives” in this present-simple conditional clause.

checks.prompt: Does “Even if the shop is closed, I will go” prove it is closed?

options.text: No. It proves the shop is open.
options.feedback: The sentence does not establish whether the shop is open or closed.

options.text: No. The closure is treated as a condition.
options.feedback: The sentence does not establish its truth.

options.text: Yes. Even if asserts that the shop is closed.
options.feedback: “Even if” presents the closure as a condition, not an established fact.

application.prompt: The weather may be bad, but you will go to class either way. Which sentence expresses that plan?

options.text: Even if the weather is bad, I will go to class.
options.feedback: “Even if” presents a possible difficulty that will not change the plan.

options.text: Even though the weather is bad, I will go to class.
options.feedback: “Even though” presents bad weather as a fact; the prompt gives it as a possibility.

options.text: If the weather is bad, I will stay home.
options.feedback: This changes the plan when the weather is bad.

concepts.title: Care about and care for
concepts.goal: Say what matters to you and who you look after.
