rules: “Care about” commonly means consider important: “I care about the environment”. “Care for” can mean look after: “She cares for her father”. “Take care of” also means look after or deal with.

“Care for” can mean like or want in some contexts: “I do not care for this music”; “Would you care for some tea?” These uses are often more formal. “I do not care” can sound dismissive, so choose a clearer phrase when you simply have no preference.

cards.label: IMPORTANCE
cards.example: I care about the result.
cards.note: The result matters to me.

cards.label: LOOK AFTER
cards.example: I care for my grandmother.
cards.note: I help look after her.

cards.label: NO PREFERENCE
cards.example: Either time works for me.
cards.note: A considerate alternative to “I do not care”.

checks.prompt: Choose the phrase that expresses concern for an issue: “We care ___ clean water.”

options.feedback: This expresses importance or concern.
“Care about” introduces a concern or issue; “care of” does not fit this verb phrase.
“Care to” normally takes a verb, as in “care to join”, not the noun phrase “clean water”.

checks.prompt: “He cares for his elderly neighbor by cooking meals and helping with daily tasks.” What does “cares for” mean here?

options.feedback: The context describes providing care.
The phrase describes giving care, not seeking advice.
“Cares for his elderly neighbor” here means looks after the neighbor.

checks.prompt: Choose an alternative to “I do not care” when either restaurant is fine.

options.text: Either restaurant is fine with me.
options.feedback: This makes it clear that you have no preference between the two restaurants, without sounding dismissive.
This rejects both restaurants; the intended meaning accepts either.

options.text: I strongly prefer the first restaurant.
options.feedback: This expresses a preference, whereas the intended meaning is no preference.

application.prompt: Punctuality matters to you, but you accept either cafe. Which pair communicates both points?

options.text: I care about arriving on time. Neither cafe is acceptable.
options.feedback: “Neither” rejects both cafes, contrary to the stated preference.

options.text: I care about arriving on time. Either cafe works for me.
options.feedback: “Care about” expresses the concern; “either cafe” accepts both options.

options.text: I do not care about arriving on time. Either cafe works for me.
options.feedback: This denies the stated importance of punctuality.

concepts.title: Success, succeed, successful, successfully
concepts.goal: Use the correct member of a word family.
rules: “Success” is a noun: “The event was a success”. “Succeed” is a verb: “We succeeded”. “Successful” is an adjective: “The event was successful”. “Successfully” is an adverb: “We completed it successfully”.

Use “succeed in” + “-ing” for achieving an action: “succeed in finding a solution”. Not every noun use needs an article: “hard work can contribute to success”. Describe what the success means instead of relying only on a positive label.

cards.label: NOUN
cards.example: The event was a success.
cards.note: “A success” names a successful event.

cards.label: VERB
cards.example: We succeeded in finding a room.
cards.note: “In” is followed by an “-ing” form.

cards.label: ADVERB
cards.example: We booked the room successfully.
cards.note: “Successfully” modifies “booked”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “The project was ___ .” (“success” / “successful”)

options.feedback: An adjective describes the project.
“Successfully” is an adverb; “was” needs “successful” or “a success” here.
Without an article, this position needs “successful”; “a success” is another valid pattern.

checks.prompt: Complete: “We succeeded in ___ the problem.” (“solve”)

options.feedback: After “in”, use the “-ing” form “solving”.
Use “succeeded in solving”, not “in to solve”.
Use “-ing” after “in”.

checks.prompt: Choose the adverb: “success” / “successful” / “successfully”

options.feedback: The adverb can describe how an action was completed.
“Success” is a noun, not an adverb.
“Successful” is an adjective; “successfully” is the adverb.

application.prompt: Which pair uses the “success” word family correctly to describe an achievement?

options.text: We successfully organized the meeting. It was a success because everyone could join.
options.feedback: “Successfully” modifies “organized”; “a success” is a noun phrase.

options.text: We successful organized the meeting. It was a success.
options.feedback: Use the adverb “successfully” to modify “organized”.

options.text: We successfully organized the meeting. It was a successfully.
options.feedback: After “a”, use the noun “success” rather than the adverb.

concepts.title: Could and was able to
concepts.goal: Distinguish past ability from a particular achievement.
rules: “Could” commonly describes a general past ability: “At ten, I could swim”. For an actual achievement on one particular occasion, “was/were able to” or “managed to” is usually clearer: “We were able to catch the last train”.

The distinction is not absolute. “Could” is natural for particular past perceptions or mental states: “I could hear music”. “Could not” can describe a specific failure: “I could not open the door”. “Could” also expresses possibility and polite requests in other contexts.

cards.label: GENERAL ABILITY
cards.example: I could read when I was five.
cards.note: A skill at a past age.

cards.label: ACHIEVEMENT
cards.example: We managed to finish before noon.
cards.note: A successful result on an occasion.

cards.label: PERCEPTION
cards.example: I could hear the train coming.
cards.note: A natural use for a particular past perception.

checks.prompt: Choose for a skill you had as a child: “When I was seven, I ___ swim.”

options.feedback: “Will” refers to the future here. “At seven” describes an ability in childhood, so use “could”.
“Can” describes present ability. This sentence describes a childhood skill in the past.
“Could” describes a general past ability. “Was able to” can also express past ability.

checks.prompt: Choose the phrase that reports an actual success: “Yesterday, we ___ get the last two tickets.”

options.feedback: “Tried to” reports the attempt, not whether it succeeded. “Managed to” states the successful result.
“Hoped to” tells us what they wanted, but it does not say they succeeded in getting the tickets.
“Managed to” reports an actual successful result. “Were able to” can also express that meaning.

checks.prompt: Is “I could hear a bell outside” natural?

options.text: Yes. Could commonly occurs with perception verbs.
options.feedback: Do not apply the achievement rule to every past use.

options.text: No. Hear must always be in a continuous form.
options.feedback: “Could hear” is a normal way to describe a past perception.

options.text: No. Could can only describe general skills.
options.feedback: “Could” is also natural with perception verbs such as “hear”.

application.prompt: Which pair reports a general childhood ability and then a specific successful result yesterday?

options.text: I could cycle when I was young. Yesterday I managed to repair a flat tire.
options.feedback: “Could” describes the past skill; “managed to” reports the successful repair.

options.text: I will cycle when I was young. Yesterday I managed to repair a flat tire.
options.feedback: “Will” does not express the childhood ability in the past.

options.text: I could cycle when I was young. Yesterday I could have repaired a flat tire, but I did not.
options.feedback: The second sentence explicitly says the repair was not done, so it is not a successful result.

concepts.title: Speak, talk, say, and tell
concepts.goal: Choose a verb that fits the message and listener.
rules: “Say” focuses on the words or message: “She said hello”; “she said that she was busy”. “Tell” commonly names the listener directly: “She told me that she was busy”. Use “say something to someone”, not “say someone something”.

“Speak” and “talk” often overlap for conversation. “Speak” is common with languages: “speak Arabic”. “Talk about” introduces a topic. Learn common exceptions as phrases: “tell a story”, “tell the truth”, “speak to someone”, “talk to or with someone”.

cards.label: MESSAGE
cards.example: She said the meeting was canceled.
cards.note: The focus is the message.

cards.label: LISTENER
cards.example: She told me the meeting was canceled.
cards.note: “Me” identifies the listener.

cards.label: TOPIC
cards.example: We talked about the schedule.
cards.note: “About” introduces the topic.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “She said me the answer.”

options.text: She said me to the answer.
options.feedback: “Say” does not take a person directly in this pattern. Use “She told me the answer”.

options.text: She told to me the answer.
options.feedback: “Tell” takes the recipient directly here: “told me the answer”.
Alternatively: “She said the answer to me”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “Do you ___ Korean?”

options.feedback: “Speak” is the usual verb for language ability.
“Speak” is used for knowing or using a language.
“Tell” normally communicates a message; “speak Korean” names a language ability.

checks.prompt: Does “tell” always need a listener?

options.text: No. Tell can never name a listener.
options.feedback: “Tell me” and “tell the team” are normal patterns.

options.text: Yes. Every use must name a listener.
options.feedback: Expressions such as “tell the truth” do not need an explicit listener.

options.text: No. Common phrases include tell a story and tell the truth.
options.feedback: Learn the whole phrase with its meaning.

application.prompt: Your colleague gave you a message about a new room. Which report is grammatical and names the recipient?

options.text: My colleague said me that the room had changed.
options.feedback: “Say” does not take “me” directly in this pattern; use “told me” or “said to me”.

options.text: My colleague told to me that the room had changed.
options.feedback: “Tell” takes the recipient directly here: “told me”.

options.text: My colleague told me that the room had changed.
options.feedback: “Told me” names the recipient and introduces the reported message.

concepts.title: Most and almost
concepts.goal: Distinguish a majority from something nearly true.
rules: “Most” before a plural or uncountable noun means the majority or greatest part: “most students”, “most water”. Use “most of” before a determiner or pronoun: “most of the students”; “most of them”.

“Almost” means nearly: “almost ready”, “almost all”, “almost everyone”. It does not normally directly modify a plural noun to mean the majority: say “most people” or “almost all people”, depending on your meaning. “Almost all” is stronger than “most”.

cards.label: MAJORITY
cards.example: Most students came.
cards.note: More than half came; the precise number is unstated.

cards.label: NEARLY EVERYONE
cards.example: Almost all the students came.
cards.note: Very few were absent.

cards.label: NEARLY A STATE
cards.example: The room is almost ready.
cards.note: Some preparation remains.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “Almost people arrived on time.”

options.feedback: If nearly everyone arrived on time, use “Almost all the people” instead.

options.text: Most people almosts arrived on time.
options.feedback: “Almost” does not take an “-s” ending, and the intended claim is about most people.

options.text: Almost of the people arrived on time.
options.feedback: Use “most of the people” or “almost all of the people”, not “almost of”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “Most ___ them agreed.”

options.feedback: Use “of” between “most” and an object pronoun such as “them”.
“Most of them” identifies a proportion of that group.
Use “of” before a pronoun such as “them”.

checks.prompt: Which suggests a larger share: “most” / “almost all”?

options.feedback: “Most” means more than half and “almost all” means nearly everyone or everything.
“Most” means a majority; “almost all” normally suggests close to the whole group.
It means nearly the entire group.

application.prompt: Which pair correctly describes a majority of classmates and a nearly finished project?

options.text: Most of my classmates walk to school. Our project is almost finished.
options.feedback: “Most of” refers to a proportion of the group; “almost” means nearly.

options.text: Almost my classmates walk to school. Our project is almost finished.
options.feedback: Use “most of my classmates” or “almost all of my classmates”.

options.text: Most of my classmates walk to school. Our project is most finished.
options.feedback: Use “almost finished” to mean nearly complete.

concepts.title: Affect and effect
concepts.goal: Describe an influence and its result.
rules: “Affect” is usually a verb meaning “influence”: “The noise affected my sleep”. “Effect” is usually a noun meaning a result or “influence”: “The noise had an effect on my sleep”.

There are less common meanings: “effect” can be a formal verb meaning “bring about”, as in “effect change”; “affect” can be a specialist noun about outward emotional expression. Start with the common patterns, but do not treat the spelling distinction as exceptionless. A causal claim still needs evidence.

cards.label: VERB
cards.example: The delay affected our plans.
cards.note: “Affected” tells what the delay did.

cards.label: NOUN
cards.example: The delay had an effect on our plans.
cards.note: “Effect” is the noun after “an”.

cards.label: CAUTIOUS CLAIM
cards.example: The delay may affect our plans.
cards.note: “May” preserves uncertainty.

checks.prompt: Choose the verb meaning “influence”: “The weather can ___ travel.”

options.feedback: A verb is needed after “can”.
“Affection” is a noun meaning fondness, not the verb “influence”.
The usual verb meaning “influence” is “affect”; “effect” as a verb means “bring about”.

checks.prompt: Choose the noun meaning “result”: “What ___ did the change have?”

options.feedback: This sentence needs the noun “effect” meaning result or “influence”.
“Effective” is an adjective; the question asks what effect the change had.
This question asks about the result as a noun.

checks.prompt: Is “effect” never a verb?

options.text: No. Effect change means bring change about.
options.feedback: That formal use is less common than the noun.

options.text: No. As a verb, effect always means notice.
options.feedback: The verb “effect” means “bring about”, not notice.

options.text: Yes. Effect is only ever a noun.
options.feedback: “Effect” can be a formal verb meaning “bring about”, as in “effect change”.

application.prompt: The timetable’s influence on your journey is uncertain. Which sentence preserves that uncertainty?

options.text: The new timetable may affect my journey to work.
options.feedback: “May” keeps the outcome possible rather than certain, and “affect” means “influence”.

options.text: The new timetable will definitely shorten my journey to work.
options.feedback: This asserts a particular outcome and certainty not provided in the prompt.

options.text: The new timetable may affection my journey to work.
options.feedback: “Affection” is a noun, not the verb needed after “may”.

concepts.title: Look, watch, hear, and listen
concepts.goal: Describe attention and perception.
rules: “Look at” directs visual attention toward something. “Watch” usually involves attention over time, often to something changing or moving. “Hear” describes receiving sound; “listen” emphasizes paying attention to it.

Use “to” before the object of “listen”: “listen to music”. “Hear” does not need “to” before its object. The attention distinction is useful but not absolute: “hear a speaker” can also mean attend a talk. Learn familiar activity phrases such as “watch television” and “look at a photo”.

cards.label: DIRECT ATTENTION
cards.example: Look at this photo.
cards.note: Turn your attention to it.

cards.label: OVER TIME
cards.example: We watched the match.
cards.note: Follow an event as it develops.

cards.label: SOUND
cards.example: I heard music and stopped to listen to it.
cards.note: The sound was perceived, then attended to.

checks.prompt: Complete: “Please listen ___ the announcement.”

options.feedback: “Listen” takes “to” before the thing you intentionally attend to.
“Listen” takes “to” before the object.
Use “listen to the announcement” without “for”.

checks.prompt: Choose the verb for viewing the game as it happened: “We ___ the game.”

options.feedback: “Watch” is natural for following a game.
“Listen” would need “to” and would describe attending to sound rather than watching.
With “the game” as the direct object, “watch” fits. “Look” would need “at”.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “I heard to a loud noise.”

options.feedback: “Listen” needs “to”; “hear” takes its object directly.

options.text: I heard at a loud noise.
options.feedback: “Hear” takes “a loud noise” directly, without “at”.
“Hear” takes the object directly.

application.prompt: You first noticed a voice, then paid attention to an announcement. Which pair fits?

options.text: I heard a voice outside. I listened the announcement.
options.feedback: “Listen” needs “to” before the object.

options.text: I heard a voice outside. I listened to the announcement.
options.feedback: “Heard” describes noticing sound; “listened to” describes deliberate attention.

options.text: I heard to a voice outside. I listened to the announcement.
options.feedback: “Hear” takes its object directly, without “to”.

concepts.title: So and such
concepts.goal: Add emphasis using the right sentence pattern.
rules: Use “so” before an adjective or adverb: “so helpful”, “so quickly”. Use “such” before a noun phrase: “such a helpful person”, “such helpful people”. With a singular countable noun, keep “a” or “an”.

Use “so” with “many”, “much”, “few”, and “little” when these describe quantities: “so many books”, “so little time”. A following “that” clause can give a result: “It was so noisy that I left”. Emphasis is a choice, not a factual measurement.

cards.label: ADJECTIVE
cards.example: The guide was so helpful.
cards.note: “So” modifies “helpful”.

cards.label: NOUN PHRASE
cards.example: She was such a helpful guide.
cards.note: “Such” introduces the noun phrase.

cards.label: QUANTITY
cards.example: There were so many questions.
cards.note: “So” combines with “many”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “It was ___ a useful lesson.”

options.feedback: “Such as” introduces examples, not this degree expression.
Use “such” before a noun phrase with “a”: “such a useful lesson”.
“A useful lesson” is a noun phrase.

checks.prompt: Complete: “The room was ___ quiet.”

options.feedback: Before the adjective “quiet” alone, use “so”.
“Such a” needs a following noun phrase, such as “such a quiet room”.
“Quiet” is an adjective without a following noun.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “We had such much work.”

options.feedback: The pattern is “so much work”.
Use “so” before the quantity word “much”.
“Work” is uncountable in this meaning, so use “much” rather than “many”.

application.prompt: Which sentence uses “so” correctly and gives the result of clear instructions?

options.text: The instructions were so clearly that I finished without help.
options.feedback: “Were” needs the adjective “clear” for this description, not the adverb “clearly”.

options.text: The instructions were so clear that I finished without help.
options.feedback: “So” modifies the adjective “clear”; “that” introduces the result.

options.text: The instructions were such clear that I finished without help.
options.feedback: Use “so” before “clear” alone, or “such clear instructions” with a noun.

concepts.title: Refuse and reject
concepts.goal: Decline an action or turn down an offer.
rules: “Refuse” can take “to” + verb: “I refused to sign”. It can also take an offer or request: “refuse an invitation”. “Reject” commonly takes a noun naming something not accepted: “reject a proposal”, “reject an application”.

Do not use “reject to do” for declining an action. Either verb can sound strong depending on context. “Decline” is often a courteous choice for an invitation. State a reason or an alternative when it helps the conversation, without inventing one.

cards.label: ACTION
cards.example: She refused to sign the form.
cards.note: “Refuse” takes a to-infinitive.

cards.label: PROPOSAL
cards.example: They rejected the proposal.
cards.note: “Reject” takes the proposal as its object.

cards.label: INVITATION
cards.example: Thank you, but I must decline.
cards.note: A courteous way to turn down an invitation.

checks.prompt: Complete: “He refused ___ answer.”

options.feedback: Use “refused to answer”, not “refused from answer”.
“Refuse” takes a to-infinitive for the action: “refused to answer”.
Use “refuse to do something”.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “They rejected to meet us.”

options.feedback: “Refuse” needs “to” before the infinitive: “refused to meet”.
This is not a correct replacement for the stated decision not to meet.
“Reject” does not take this to-infinitive pattern.

checks.prompt: Can “refuse” take a noun?

options.text: No. Refuse must always take a to-infinitive.
options.feedback: “Refuse” can take a noun, such as “help” or “an invitation”.

options.text: Yes: refuse an invitation or refuse help.
options.feedback: Its patterns are broader than “refuse to do”.

options.text: Yes, but only the noun answer.
options.feedback: Many nouns can follow “refuse”, including “help” and “an invitation”.

application.prompt: You cannot attend an event and have given no reason. Which reply declines politely without inventing one?

options.text: Thank you for inviting me. I look forward to joining you.
options.feedback: This accepts the invitation rather than declining.

options.text: Thank you for inviting me, but I cannot join because I am ill.
options.feedback: The prompt does not establish illness; the reply invents a reason.

options.text: Thank you for inviting me, but I cannot join you this time.
options.feedback: This declines courteously without adding an unsupported explanation.

concepts.title: Explain an unfamiliar idea
concepts.goal: Help a listener understand a new term.
rules: Start with a familiar category, then describe the defining feature and give a concrete example: “A commuter is a person who regularly travels between home and work”. The example should clarify the definition, not replace it.

Adjust the detail to the listener. Ask what they already know and check understanding with a useful question. Avoid explaining one unfamiliar word through several more unfamiliar words. An analogy helps only if you also state where it differs.

cards.label: CATEGORY
cards.example: A library is a place where people can borrow books.
cards.note: Start with a familiar kind of thing.

cards.label: EXAMPLE
cards.example: You can borrow a novel and return it later.
cards.note: Make the activity concrete.

cards.label: CHECK
cards.example: How is borrowing different from buying?
cards.note: Ask about the important distinction.

checks.prompt: Which opening is clearer for a beginner: “A commuter is a person ...” / “A commuter is an intermodal participant ...”?

options.text: Both are equally easy for every beginner.
options.feedback: A simple familiar category such as “person” gives a beginner a clearer starting point.

options.text: A commuter is an intermodal participant ...
options.feedback: This replaces an unfamiliar word with another difficult expression.
A familiar category gives the listener a starting point.

checks.prompt: Which sentence explains “borrow”?

options.text: Borrow means give someone something for a time.
options.feedback: That describes “lend” from the owner’s perspective, not “borrow” from the user’s.

options.text: Borrow means use something for a time and then return it.
options.feedback: Include the temporary use and expected return.

options.text: Borrow means keep something permanently without returning it.
options.feedback: Borrowing normally involves temporary use and returning the item.

checks.prompt: Why might an example alone be insufficient?

options.text: It may not show what all uses have in common.
options.feedback: A short definition gives the general meaning.

options.text: An example always gives a complete definition.
options.feedback: An example illustrates one case and may leave the wider meaning unclear.
Examples can help, especially alongside a short general explanation.

application.prompt: Which explanation gives a beginner a simple category and the basic use of a delivery locker?

options.text: A delivery locker is an asynchronous fulfillment endpoint.
options.feedback: This relies on difficult technical terms and gives no simple action.

options.text: A delivery locker is a secure place to collect a package. You use a code to open its door.
options.feedback: The explanation identifies the kind of place and gives a concrete action.

options.text: A delivery locker is a place where you buy a package and choose its contents.
options.feedback: This confuses collecting a delivered package with shopping.

concepts.title: Describing trends
concepts.goal: Describe a change with its amount and time period.
rules: Use “rise”, “increase”, “fall”, or “decrease” for direction. Use “remain stable” for little change and “fluctuate” for repeated movement up and down. A number without a time period or unit can be misleading.

Distinguish “rise by” from “rise to”: from 40 to 50 is a rise by 10, ending at 50. A change from 20% to 25% is five percentage points, or a 25% relative increase. Describe the data separately from an explanation of its cause.

cards.label: START AND END
cards.example: Attendance rose from 40 people to 50 people in June.
cards.note: The unit is people; the period is June.

cards.label: AMOUNT
cards.example: Attendance rose by 10.
cards.note: “By” introduces the size of the change.

cards.label: LIMIT
cards.example: The figures rose, but the cause is unclear.
cards.note: The trend alone does not establish a cause.

checks.prompt: Attendance rose from 20 to 30. How much did it rise by?

options.feedback: 30 is the final total. The increase is 30 minus 20.
20 is the starting total, not the amount of increase.
Subtract the starting count from the ending count.

checks.prompt: Sales increased from 500 units to 600 units. Which sentence gives those starting and ending values correctly?

options.feedback: This reverses the starting and finishing values and describes a fall.
“From 500 to 600” gives the stated starting and ending values. “By 500 to 600” is grammatical for a different change: from 100 to 600.
This says the increase was 600, which would give a final value of 1100.

checks.prompt: A rate rises from 10% to 12%. How many percentage points is that?

options.feedback: 12% is the final rate. Subtract 10 from 12 to find the percentage-point increase.
Subtract the percentages; the relative increase is 20%.
20% is the relative increase from 10 to 12, not the percentage-point difference.

application.prompt: Bus use increased from 80 to 100 journeys per day in July. The cause is unknown. Which report preserves those facts?

options.text: Bus use rose by 100 journeys per day in July because fares fell.
options.feedback: The increase was 20, not 100, and the cause is invented.

options.text: Bus fares rose from 80 to 100 dollars per day in July.
options.feedback: This changes both the thing measured and its unit.

options.text: Bus use rose from 80 to 100 journeys per day in July. The reason is not yet clear.
options.feedback: The report includes the values, unit, period, and uncertainty about cause.

concepts.title: Asking for and giving advice
concepts.goal: Ask a focused question and offer a useful option.
rules: Give enough context for the listener to understand the problem. State your goal or constraint, then ask a specific question: “I have ten minutes. Which route would you suggest?” “Advice” is normally uncountable: “some advice”, “a piece of advice”.

When responding, offer an option and a reason. “Could” can present a possibility; “should” can make a stronger recommendation. Ask a clarifying question when information is missing. Acknowledge limits rather than giving confident advice on something you do not know.

cards.label: CONTEXT
cards.example: I need to reach the station by nine.
cards.note: State the goal and constraint.

cards.label: QUESTION
cards.example: Which route would you recommend?
cards.note: Ask something the listener can answer.

cards.label: OPTION + REASON
cards.example: You could take the bus because it stops nearby.
cards.note: Offer an option with a relevant reason.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: “Can you give me an advice?”

options.text: Can you give me some advices?
options.feedback: “Advice” is normally uncountable, so do not add “-s”.

options.text: Can you give me some advice?
options.feedback: “Advice” is normally uncountable.

options.text: Can you give me a advice?
options.feedback: “Advice” is not normally used with “a”; use “some advice” or “a piece of advice”.

checks.prompt: Which question is more focused: “What should I do?” / “Which bus goes to the station?”

options.feedback: This gives no specific decision or goal. The bus question identifies the information needed.

options.text: Which bus goes to the station?
options.feedback: It specifies the information needed.

options.text: Both questions identify exactly the same problem.
options.feedback: Only the bus question gives a specific destination and information need.

checks.prompt: What should you do before advising if the deadline is unclear?

options.feedback: An assumption can lead to unsuitable advice. Ask about the timing.

options.text: Recommend the quickest option without asking.
options.feedback: The timing affects which advice fits the person’s needs.

options.text: Ask when the person needs to finish or arrive.
options.feedback: Clarify the missing constraint.

application.prompt: A learner needs a quiet study place. Which exchange gives a relevant option with a reason?

options.text: I need a quiet place to study. You must go somewhere immediately.
options.feedback: This gives no specific option or reason and adds unsupported urgency.

options.text: I need a quiet place to study. Try the loud music bar because it has live bands.
options.feedback: The suggested reason conflicts with the need for quiet.

options.text: I need a quiet place to study. Where would you suggest? You could try the library because it has a quiet room.
options.feedback: The question gives the need; the suggestion and reason directly address quiet study.

concepts.title: To + verb or to + -ing?
concepts.goal: Choose the verb form that fits the complete expression.
rules: After “want to”, “plan to”, and “hope to”, use the base verb: “want to learn”, “plan to study”, “hope to improve”. The base verb is the plain form, such as “learn”. The combination “to learn” is called a to-infinitive.

In “look forward to”, “object to”, and “refer to”, “to” is a preposition: a linking word that can introduce a noun or an -ing form. Compare “I look forward to the lesson” and “I look forward to learning”. Say “This refers to meeting the requirements”, not “This refers to meet the requirements”.

Learn the complete expression. Seeing “to” alone does not tell you which verb form comes next. These examples show two common patterns; they are not a rule for every phrase containing “to”. An -ing form after a preposition does not by itself mean the action is happening now: “I look forward to meeting you next week” refers to a future meeting.

cards.label: TO + BASE VERB
cards.example: I want to learn. We plan to study. They hope to improve.
cards.note: Keep the base form after “want to”, “plan to”, and “hope to”.

cards.label: TO + -ING
cards.example: I look forward to learning. She objects to working late.
cards.note: Here, “to” belongs to the expression before it. Follow it with an -ing form when naming an action.

cards.label: REFER TO + -ING
cards.example: This refers to meeting the requirements.
cards.note: “Meeting” means satisfying the requirements. “Refer to” can also take a noun: “This refers to the requirements”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “They hope to ___ more next year.”

options.feedback: After “hope to”, use the base verb “learn”, without -ing.
“Hope to” takes the base verb: “hope to learn”.
“Learned” is a past form. After “hope to”, use “learn”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “This refers to ___ the requirements.”

options.feedback: In “refer to”, “to” is a preposition. Use “meeting” to name the action.
“Met” is a past form. The required form here is “meeting”.
“Refer to” can take an -ing form. Here, “meeting the requirements” means satisfying them.

checks.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a noun after “look forward to”?

options.text: I look forward to the lesson.
options.feedback: “The lesson” is a noun phrase. Both a noun phrase and an -ing form can follow “look forward to”.
Keep “to” in the expression: “look forward to the lesson”.
“Learn” is a base verb, not a noun here. Use “learning” or the noun phrase “the lesson”.

application.prompt: You will meet a new colleague next week and want to express positive anticipation. Which closing sentence fits a work email?

options.text: We look forward to meet you next week.
options.feedback: After “look forward to”, use “meeting”, not the base verb “meet”.

options.text: We look forward to meeting you next week.
options.feedback: “Look forward to meeting” is the correct pattern. “Next week” makes the future timing clear.

options.text: We look forward meeting you next week.
options.feedback: The expression needs “to”: “look forward to meeting you”.

concepts.title: One of + plural noun
concepts.goal: Describe one member of a group with a plural noun and the right main verb.
rules: Use “one of” to select a single member from a group. The noun naming that group is plural: “one of the books”, “one of my friends”, “one of these ideas”. Keep the word that identifies the group, such as “the”, “my”, or “these”. Compare “one book” with “one of the books”.

Keep the noun plural after a describing word too: “one of the best ideas”, not “one of the best idea”. Use the correct plural form; it does not always end in -s. For example, say “one of the children”, not “one of the childs”.

When “one of …” is the subject of a simple sentence, its main verb agrees with “one”: “One of the books is missing” and “One of my friends has a bicycle”. The group noun stays plural, but we are describing one member. Compare “The books are missing” with “One of the books is missing”. This lesson covers these simple sentences; verbs inside added “who” or “that” clauses need their own analysis.

cards.label: ONE MEMBER, A PLURAL GROUP
cards.example: one book / one of the books; one friend / one of my friends
cards.note: After “one of”, name the group with a plural noun.

cards.label: AFTER A DESCRIBING WORD
cards.example: This is one of the best ideas. One of the children is smiling.
cards.note: “Ideas” remains plural after “best”. “Children” is the plural of “child”.

cards.label: THE MAIN VERB FOLLOWS ONE
cards.example: One of the books is missing. One of my friends has a bicycle.
cards.note: Use “is” and “has” for the single member, even though “books” and “friends” are plural.

checks.prompt: Complete: “I borrowed one of the ___ from the shelf.”

options.feedback: “One of” selects a member from a group. Name the group with the plural “books”.
“Books” names the group; “one of” selects a single book from it.
The apostrophe does not make a noun plural. Use “books” to name this group.

checks.prompt: Complete: “This is one of the best ___ in the town.”

options.feedback: The group noun after “one of” must be plural, even with “best” before it.
This apostrophe form is not the plural needed here. Use “cafés”.
“One of the best cafés” describes a single café within a group of excellent cafés.

checks.prompt: Complete: “One of the children ___ a red backpack.”

options.feedback: The main verb agrees with “one”: “One of the children has a red backpack”.
“Children” names the group, but the subject refers to one child. Use “has”.
The sentence says that one child possesses a backpack, so it needs “has”.

application.prompt: You and your friends planned a picnic. Exactly one friend is bringing a blanket. Which message is grammatically correct and fits the plan?

options.text: One of my friend is bringing a blanket.
options.feedback: The group noun needs its plural form: “one of my friends”.

options.text: One of my friends is bringing a blanket.
options.feedback: “Friends” names the group, and “is bringing” describes the one friend bringing the blanket.

options.text: One of my friends are bringing a blanket.
options.feedback: The main verb agrees with “one”, so use “is bringing”, not “are bringing”.

concepts.title: Don't or doesn't?
concepts.goal: Choose don't or doesn't and keep the following verb in its base form.
rules: For present-simple negatives with verbs such as “drive”, “work”, and “open”, use “don’t” with “I”, “you”, “we”, and “they”. Use “doesn’t” with “he”, “she”, and “it”. A singular noun follows the “it” pattern: “This shop doesn’t open on Sundays”. A plural noun follows “they”: “These shops don’t open on Sundays”. These are the standard-English forms taught in this lesson.

After “don’t” or “doesn’t”, use the base verb: the plain form, such as “drive”, “work”, or “open”. Compare “She drives” with “She doesn’t drive”. Do not add -s or -es to the main verb after “doesn’t”. The same pattern gives “doesn’t have” and “doesn’t go”, not “doesn’t has” or “doesn’t goes”. The full forms are “do not” and “does not”.

This pattern does not apply to every negative sentence. With “be”, put “not” after “am”, “is”, or “are”: “I am not late”, “The printer isn’t ready”, “They aren’t tired”. Compare “The printer doesn’t work” with “The printer isn’t ready”. The first uses the verb “work”; the second uses “be” with the describing word “ready”.

cards.label: I / YOU / WE / THEY: DON'T
cards.example: I don’t drive. They don’t work on Sundays.
cards.note: “Don’t” means “do not”. The following verb stays in its plain form.

cards.label: HE / SHE / IT: DOESN'T
cards.example: She doesn’t drive. This shop doesn’t open on Sundays.
cards.note: “This shop” is singular, so it follows the same pattern as “it”.

cards.label: KEEP THE BASE VERB
cards.example: She drives. / She doesn’t drive. He has a ticket. / He doesn’t have a ticket.
cards.note: “Doesn’t” carries the subject agreement. The next verb is “drive” or “have”, without a third-person ending.

checks.prompt: Complete in standard English: “My neighbors ___ own a car.”

options.feedback: “My neighbors” means more than one person and follows the “they” pattern. Use “don’t”.
“My neighbors” is plural. Use “don’t” followed by the base verb “own”.
“Own” is the main verb here. Make its present-simple negative with “don’t”, not “aren’t”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “The museum doesn’t ___ until ten.”

options.feedback: After “doesn’t”, use the base verb “open” without -s.
The form after “doesn’t” is the base verb “open”, not “opening”.
“Doesn’t” is followed by the base form: “doesn’t open”.

checks.prompt: Which sentence correctly says that the printer is not ready?

options.feedback: “Ready” describes a state. Use “is not” or “isn’t” with it.
“Ready” is a describing word in this sentence. Use “isn’t ready”.
Use “isn’t ready”. “Don’t” cannot replace “isn’t” before the describing word “ready”.

application.prompt: A friend asks whether your sister owns a bicycle. She owns none. Which reply is correct in standard English?

options.feedback: After “doesn’t”, the base verb is “have”, not “has”.
Use “doesn’t” with “she”, then the base form “have”.
In standard English, “she” takes “doesn’t”, not “don’t”.

concepts.title: Maybe or may be?
concepts.goal: Distinguish the one-word adverb “maybe” from the two-word verb phrase “may be”.
rules: “Maybe” is one word meaning “perhaps”. It is an adverb: it adds uncertainty to a statement. A useful pattern is “Maybe + subject + verb”: “Maybe the shop is open”. Keep the verb that the statement needs: “Maybe the keys are upstairs”. “Maybe” can appear in other positions too; this lesson practises the common beginning position.

“May be” is two words. “May” is a modal verb, a helping verb that can express possibility, and “be” is the plain form of the next verb. Put the subject before it: “The shop may be open”. This expresses the same possibility as “Maybe the shop is open”, using a different sentence pattern. Write “The keys may be upstairs”, not “The keys maybe upstairs”.

After “may”, use the plain verb form without “to” or a third-person -s: “She may arrive early”. With the verb “be”, use “may be”, not “may is” or “may are”. These examples express possibility, not certainty; they do not assign an exact percentage. They can describe now (“The shop may be open now”) or the future (“The shop may be open tomorrow”). “May” also has other uses, such as permission, which this lesson does not cover.

cards.label: MAYBE: ONE WORD
cards.example: Maybe the shop is open. Maybe the keys are upstairs.
cards.note: “Maybe” means “perhaps”. The statements still need their verbs: “is” and “are”.

cards.label: MAY BE: TWO WORDS
cards.example: The shop may be open. The keys may be upstairs.
cards.note: The subject comes before “may be”. Keep a space between the helping verb “may” and the plain verb “be”.

cards.label: MAY + PLAIN VERB
cards.example: She may arrive early. The shop may be open tomorrow.
cards.note: Use “arrive” or “be” after “may”. Do not add “to”, -s, or a form such as “is”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “___ the museum is open today.”

options.feedback: The statement already has its verb “is”. Put the one-word adverb “Maybe” before “the museum”.
“Maybe” means “perhaps” and introduces the statement “the museum is open today”.
“May” cannot introduce this statement before its subject. Use “Maybe the museum is open”.

checks.prompt: Complete: “The museum ___ open today.”

options.feedback: “Maybe” cannot supply the missing verb. Use “may be”, or rewrite the sentence as “Maybe the museum is open today”.
After “may”, use the plain verb “be”, not “is”.
The subject “the museum” is followed by “may” and the plain verb “be”.

checks.prompt: Which sentence correctly expresses a possible early arrival?

options.feedback: “May” is followed by the plain verb “arrive”, without -s or “to”.
Do not add -s to the verb after “may”. Use “may arrive”.
“May” takes the plain verb without “to”: “may arrive”.

application.prompt: You are unsure where the keys are. Which sentence correctly expresses the same possibility as “Maybe the keys are upstairs”?

options.feedback: “Maybe” is an adverb, so this sentence is missing a verb. Write “The keys may be upstairs”.
This uses “may” plus “be” to express the same possible location.
Use the plain form “be” after “may”, even with the plural subject “the keys”.

concepts.title: Spend time: on, with, or -ing?
concepts.goal: Use “spend time on” for a task, “spend time with” for company, and “spend time doing” to name an activity.
rules: Use “spend + time + on + task” to describe time devoted to a task: “I spent an hour on the report”. The time phrase can be “an hour”, “ten minutes”, or simply “time”. The past form of “spend” is “spent”; the present forms are “spend” and “spends”.

Use “spend + time + with + person” when the meaning is time together: “I spent an hour with my sister”. Choose the preposition for the relationship you mean. “On a task” and “with a person” are useful patterns, not a universal rule that objects always take “on” and people always take “with”.

To say what you did during that time, use an -ing form: “I spent an hour reading”. Do not replace “reading” with “to read” in this pattern. You can combine activity and company: “I spent an hour reading with my sister”. “On + -ing” is also possible. Place phrases work too, as in “We spent the afternoon in the garden”.

cards.label: ON: A TASK
cards.example: I spent an hour on the report.
cards.note: This tells us which task received the time and attention.

cards.label: WITH: TIME TOGETHER
cards.example: I spent an hour with my sister.
cards.note: This tells us who was there with the speaker.

cards.label: -ING: THE ACTIVITY
cards.example: I spent an hour reading.
cards.note: This tells us what the speaker did. Use “reading”, not “to read”, to name that activity.

checks.prompt: You worked on a poster for thirty minutes. Complete: “I spent thirty minutes ___ the poster.”

options.feedback: “Of” does not introduce the task after “spent thirty minutes”. Use “on the poster”.
“On the poster” names the task that received thirty minutes of work.
Use “on” before this task: “spent thirty minutes on the poster”.

checks.prompt: You enjoyed an afternoon together with your cousin. Complete: “I spent the afternoon ___ my cousin.”

options.feedback: “At my cousin” does not express time together. Use “with my cousin”.
“Of” does not identify your companion in this sentence. Use “with”.
“With my cousin” expresses who shared the afternoon with you.

checks.prompt: You listened to a podcast for twenty minutes. Which sentence correctly names that activity after “spent”?

options.text: I spent twenty minutes listening to a podcast.
options.feedback: “Listening” is the -ing form that names the activity during those twenty minutes.

options.text: I spent twenty minutes to listen to a podcast.
options.feedback: To name the activity in this pattern, use “listening”, not “to listen”.

options.text: I spent twenty minutes listen to a podcast.
options.feedback: The plain verb “listen” does not fit here. Use the -ing form “listening”.

application.prompt: You and your classmates worked together on a model for two hours. Which sentence correctly identifies both the task and your companions?

options.text: We spent two hours with the model on our classmates.
options.feedback: This reverses the intended relationships. The task is “on the model”; the company is “with our classmates”.

options.text: We spent two hours on the model with our classmates.
options.feedback: “On the model” names the task; “with our classmates” identifies the people working together.

options.text: We spent two hours to the model of our classmates.
options.feedback: Use “on” for this task and “with” for the people sharing the time.

concepts.title: Talking about jobs: a or an?
concepts.goal: Introduce a person’s job with “a” or “an”, choosing the article by the next word’s first sound.
rules: When introducing one person’s job, we usually use “a” or “an” before the singular job noun: “She is a teacher”; “She is an engineer”. Keep the article after “work as” too: “He works as a designer”. “A” and “an” are articles: small words that introduce the noun phrase. In these ordinary introductions, do not say “I work as teacher”.

Choose by the first sound of the word immediately after the article. Use “a” before a consonant sound: “a teacher”, “a designer”. Use “an” before a vowel sound: “an engineer”, “an artist”. An adjective can change the choice: “a teacher” but “an experienced teacher”. The first sound of “experienced”, not “teacher”, now decides the article.

Sound and spelling do not always match. “University” starts with the consonant sound at the beginning of “you”, so say “a university teacher”. For plural job nouns, leave out “a/an”: “They are teachers”. Use “the” when identifying a particular person, as in “She is the teacher I told you about”. Titles and appointment expressions can have other patterns, such as “elected president”; this lesson practises ordinary job introductions.

cards.label: A: CONSONANT SOUND
cards.example: She is a teacher. He works as a designer.
cards.note: The next words, “teacher” and “designer”, begin with consonant sounds.

cards.label: AN: VOWEL SOUND
cards.example: She is an engineer. He works as an artist.
cards.note: The next words, “engineer” and “artist”, begin with vowel sounds.

cards.label: LISTEN TO THE NEXT WORD
cards.example: a university teacher; an experienced teacher
cards.note: “University” begins with a “you” sound. “Experienced” begins with a vowel sound.

checks.prompt: You are introducing your job. Complete: “I am ___ mechanic.”

options.feedback: “Mechanic” begins with the consonant sound /m/. Use “a mechanic”.
Keep the article in this job introduction. “Mechanic” begins with a consonant sound, so use “a”.
This ordinary singular job introduction needs an article: “I am a mechanic”.

checks.prompt: Which sentence correctly introduces someone’s job?

options.feedback: “Engineer” starts with a vowel sound. Use “an engineer”.
Keep the article after “works as”: “She works as an engineer”.
“An” introduces the singular job noun “engineer”, which starts with a vowel sound.

checks.prompt: Complete this job description: “He is ___ university teacher.”

options.feedback: “University” starts with the consonant sound in “you”, even though its first letter is u. Use “a”.
Choose by sound, not just the letter u. Say “a university teacher”.
Keep the article in this introduction: “He is a university teacher”.

application.prompt: You are a designer with several years of experience. Which sentence introduces your job correctly?

options.text: I work as a experienced designer.
options.feedback: The word immediately after the article is “experienced”, which begins with a vowel sound. Use “an”.

options.text: I work as an experienced designer.
options.feedback: Use “an” before the vowel sound at the beginning of “experienced”. The later word “designer” does not decide the article.
The adjective does not remove the need for an article. Say “an experienced designer”.

concepts.title: Do or does? Asking everyday questions
concepts.goal: Ask present-simple questions with “do” or “does” and keep the main verb in its base form.
rules: For ordinary present-simple questions with most main verbs, put “do” or “does” before the subject, the person or thing the question is about. Use “do” with I, you, we, and they: “Do you like music?” Use “does” with he, she, it, or one named person or thing: “Does she like music?”; “Does the shop open early?”

After “do” or “does”, use the base verb, the form without an added -s: “She likes music” becomes “Does she like music?” Do not say “Does she likes music?” Put a question word before “do” or “does” when asking for information: “Where do they work?”; “When does the bus leave?” Short answers repeat the helping verb: “Yes, she does”; “No, she doesn’t”.

This pattern does not cover every question. With “be”, move the verb before the subject: “Is she busy?” With a modal verb, a helping verb such as “can”, ask “Can she swim?” Do not add “do” to either pattern. When “who” or “what” itself is the subject, an ordinary neutral question usually needs no “do” or “does”: “Who works here?” Compare “Who does she work with?”, where “she” is the subject. This lesson practises direct present-simple questions with most main verbs.

cards.label: DO + SUBJECT + BASE VERB
cards.example: Do you like music? Where do they work?
cards.note: Use “do” with I, you, we, and they. A question word goes before “do”.

cards.label: DOES + SUBJECT + BASE VERB
cards.example: Does she like music? When does the bus leave?
cards.note: Use “does” with he, she, it, or one named person or thing. Keep “like” and “leave” in the base form.

cards.label: MOVE THE -S TO DOES
cards.example: She likes music. → Does she like music?
cards.note: “Does” carries the present-simple third-person form. Do not add another -s to “like”.

checks.prompt: Ask about your friends’ usual travel. Complete: “___ they walk to school?”

options.feedback: “They” takes “do”, not “does”, in this present-simple question.
Use “do” before “they”, followed by the base verb “walk”.
“Are they walk” is not the present-simple question pattern. Use “Do they walk”.

checks.prompt: Which question correctly asks about her usual reading?

options.feedback: After “does”, use the base verb “read”, without -s.
“She” takes “does”, not “do”, in a present-simple question.
“Does” comes before “she”, and “read” stays in its base form.

checks.prompt: Ask about a café’s regular closing time. Which question is correct?

options.feedback: Put “when” first, then “does”, the subject “the café”, and the base verb “close”.
For this direct question, put “does” before “the café”: “When does the café close?”
Use “close”, not “closes”, after “does”.

application.prompt: Your friend says, “My brother works in a hospital.” Ask about his usual starting time. Which direct question is correct?

options.text: What time does he starts work?
options.feedback: “Does” already carries the third-person form. Use “start”, without -s.

options.text: What time does he start work?
options.feedback: The order is question phrase + does + subject + base verb: “What time does he start work?”
An ordinary direct question with “start” needs “does” before “he” and the base verb “start”.

concepts.title: Fewer or less? Comparing quantities
concepts.goal: Compare a smaller number or amount with “fewer” and “less”, and recognize common measurement expressions.
rules: Use “fewer” for a smaller number of separate things: “We need fewer boxes.” The noun is plural because boxes are countable: one box, two boxes. In careful writing, choose “fewer” with ordinary plural countable nouns such as mistakes, bottles, and questions.

Use “less” for a smaller amount: “We need less paper”; “This takes less time.” Paper and time are uncountable in these examples. If you name countable units, change the word: “less water” but “fewer bottles of water”; “less paper” but “fewer sheets of paper”. The noun you choose determines the pattern.

This is a useful starting rule, not an absolute ban on “less” with plurals. Measurements commonly use “less”: “less than ten minutes”, “less than twenty dollars”. The words describe a total amount of time or money. You may also hear “less” with ordinary plural nouns in conversation; “fewer” is the safer choice for those nouns in careful writing. “Fewer” and “less” make comparisons; they do not necessarily mean that the remaining quantity is small.

cards.label: FEWER: A SMALLER NUMBER
cards.example: We need fewer boxes. She made fewer mistakes.
cards.note: Boxes and mistakes are separate things we can count. Use the plural noun after “fewer”.

cards.label: LESS: A SMALLER AMOUNT
cards.example: We need less paper. This takes less time.
cards.note: Paper is a material here, and time is an amount. Neither noun needs a plural ending in these examples.

cards.label: CHECK THE NOUN AND THE MEANING
cards.example: fewer bottles • less water • less than ten minutes
cards.note: Bottles are counted as objects. Water is measured as an amount. A time measurement can also describe one total amount.

checks.prompt: There were eight delivery boxes yesterday and five today. Which sentence uses the usual careful-writing pattern for a smaller number?

options.feedback: Five is a smaller number than eight. “Fewer” goes with the plural countable noun “boxes”.
Use the plural noun “boxes” after “fewer”.
“More” describes a larger number, but five is smaller than eight.

checks.prompt: The printer now uses a smaller amount of paper. Complete: “The printer uses ___ paper.”

options.feedback: “Paper” names an uncountable material here. Use “less paper”, or name units: “fewer sheets of paper”.
“Less paper” describes a smaller amount of the material.
“Many” needs a plural countable noun, such as “sheets”, and does not express a smaller amount.

checks.prompt: A journey takes eight minutes. Which sentence correctly expresses that its total duration is below ten minutes?

options.text: It takes more than ten minutes.
options.feedback: Eight minutes is below ten, so “more than ten” gives the wrong information.
Add “than” before the comparison point: “less than ten minutes”.

options.text: It takes less than ten minutes.
options.feedback: This is a standard measurement expression. “Less than” compares the total duration with ten minutes.

application.prompt: Last week a kitchen used twelve bottles and six litres of water. This week it used eight bottles and four litres. Choose the sentence that accurately compares both quantities in careful written English.

options.text: The kitchen used fewer bottles and fewer water.
options.feedback: “Fewer bottles” is right, but water is uncountable in this sentence. Use “less water”.

options.text: The kitchen used fewer bottles and less water.
options.feedback: The number of bottles fell from twelve to eight, and the amount of water fell from six to four litres.

options.text: The kitchen used more bottles and less water.
options.feedback: The amount of water decreased, but so did the number of bottles. Use “fewer bottles”, not “more bottles”.

concepts.title: Leaves or leave? Matching subjects and verbs
concepts.goal: Choose the correct verb form in present-simple statements by matching it to the subject.
rules: In present-simple statements, a singular subject that could be replaced by he, she, or it usually takes a verb ending in -s: “The train leaves at six”; “The shop opens early.” This matching is called subject–verb agreement. Use the present simple for habits, general facts, and regular schedules. These examples describe a timetable and a usual opening time.

With a plural subject, use the base form: “The trains leave at six”; “The shops open early.” The base form is the plain verb, such as leave or open. A plural noun may end in -s, but its present-simple verb does not take the he/she/it ending. I, you, we, and they also take the base form: “I leave early”; “You work here.” This is true even when I or you refers to just one person.

Check the spelling: work becomes works; watch becomes watches; study becomes studies. Have becomes has with he, she, or it. Be has its own forms: I am, you/we/they are, and he/she/it is. After a modal verb such as can, use the base form: “She can swim.” This lesson focuses on affirmative statements with ordinary verbs. For do/does questions and don't/doesn't negatives, use the related lessons.

cards.label: ONE TRAIN: IT LEAVES
cards.example: The train leaves at six. The shop opens early.
cards.note: Train and shop are singular here. Each can be replaced by it, so leaves and opens have the -s ending.

cards.label: TWO TRAINS: THEY LEAVE
cards.example: The trains leave at six. The shops open early.
cards.note: Trains and shops are plural here. Each can be replaced by they. Use leave and open without the he/she/it ending.

cards.label: CHECK THE SUBJECT AND THE SPELLING
cards.example: I work. You work. She works. He watches. They study.
cards.note: I and you take the base form even when referring to one person. Some he/she/it forms need -es or a spelling change: watches, studies.

checks.prompt: Complete this statement about one shop's usual opening time: “The shop ___ at nine.”

options.feedback: The subject is one shop, so it matches it. Use the he/she/it form opens.
One shop can be replaced by it. In this present-simple statement, the verb takes -s: opens.
Opening cannot stand alone as the verb in this statement. The present-simple form is opens.

checks.prompt: Complete this statement about two trains' regular schedule: “Both trains ___ at six.”

options.feedback: The subject “both trains” is plural, like “they”. Use the base form leave.
Leaves goes with he, she, it, or a singular noun subject. Use leave with the plural subject “both trains”.
Leaving alone does not form this present-simple statement. Use leave.

checks.prompt: Choose the correct present-simple statement with the subject “I”.

options.text: I walks to the station every day.
options.feedback: Walks is the he/she/it form. Use the base form walk after “I”.

options.text: I walking to the station every day.
options.feedback: Walking cannot stand alone here. For this present-simple statement, use walk.

options.text: I walk to the station every day.
options.feedback: The pronoun “I” takes the base form walk, even though the speaker is one person.

application.prompt: One bus stops outside a station. Two other buses stop outside a school. Choose the sentence that correctly describes both regular routes.

options.text: One bus stop at the station, and two buses stops at the school.
options.feedback: The endings are reversed. “One bus” takes stops; “two buses” takes stop.

options.text: One bus stops at the station, and two buses stop at the school.
options.feedback: “One bus” matches “it”, so use stops. “Two buses” matches “they”, so use the base form stop.

options.text: One bus stops at the station, and two buses stops at the school.
options.feedback: The first verb is right. Change the second verb to stop because the subject “two buses” is plural.

concepts.title: Japan or the US? Articles with country names
concepts.goal: Use country names naturally in full sentences by choosing the or no article.
rules: Most ordinary country names take no article: “We live in Japan”; “Our flight goes to Canada”; “She is from Brazil.” No article means that you put nothing before the name. Do not add the just because you mean one particular country.

Some country names normally take the. Names containing words such as Kingdom, States, or Republic usually follow this pattern: the United Kingdom and the United States. Keep the with their common abbreviations when they name the country in a sentence: “He works in the UK”; “They live in the US.”

Learn familiar plural names with the, including the Netherlands and the Philippines: “We visited the Netherlands.” Use the established name rather than guessing from the country's size, location, or islands. These patterns describe ordinary country names used as nouns in full sentences. A country label on a map or an abbreviation before another noun, such as “US dollars”, can follow a different pattern.

cards.label: NO ARTICLE: JAPAN, CANADA, BRAZIL
cards.example: She lives in Japan. He works in Canada.
cards.note: Use these country names directly after in, to, or from. The preposition does not create a need for the.

cards.label: KEEP THE: THE US AND THE UK
cards.example: We moved to the US. Our cousins live in the UK.
cards.note: The short forms follow the country-name pattern: the United States becomes the US, and the United Kingdom becomes the UK.

cards.label: LEARN THESE NAMES TOGETHER WITH THE
cards.example: Our team visited the Netherlands. The parcel came from the Philippines.
cards.note: Both names normally take the in these full sentences. Learn the as part of each expression.

checks.prompt: Complete this ordinary statement about a place to live: “My friend lives in ___.”

options.feedback: The ordinary country name “Japan” takes no article here. Use “in Japan”.
“Japan” is normally used without an article: “My friend lives in Japan”.
You are naming the country, not one member of a countable group. Use “Japan” without an article.

checks.prompt: Use the abbreviation US to complete this full sentence: “Our office is in ___.”

options.feedback: Keep the with this country name: “the United States” and “the US”.
In this ordinary full sentence, the country name needs the: “in the US”.
This country name takes the, not a or an. Say “in the US”.

checks.prompt: Choose the usual form of the country name in this complete sentence.

options.text: We spent a week in Netherlands.
options.feedback: The country name is normally “the Netherlands”. Keep the after in.

options.text: We spent a week in a Netherlands.
options.feedback: The established country name uses the, not a: “the Netherlands”.

options.text: We spent a week in the Netherlands.
options.feedback: “The Netherlands” normally takes the when used as a country name in a full sentence.

application.prompt: Your trip starts in Canada and ends in the United Kingdom. Choose the natural full sentence using Canada and UK.

options.text: We fly from the Canada to the UK.
options.feedback: “The UK” is right, but the ordinary country name “Canada” takes no article. Say “from Canada”.

options.text: We fly from Canada to the UK.
options.feedback: Use “Canada” without an article and keep the in “the UK”.

options.text: We fly from Canada to UK.
options.feedback: “Canada” is right, but “UK” needs the in this full sentence. Say “to the UK”.
